title: Capacity Limits in Cognitive Processing Reflect the Curse of Generalization
65a5e431acc5d0a8d2c5143f2e9ef4740d73e2de.abstract: The striking constraints of some human cognitive processes stand in stark contrastto the near limitless capability of others. While we can acquire and flexibly use vast amountsof information, the amount we can process at any one time is often stiflingly limited: forexample the number of items we can hold in working memory or the number of tasks that canbe performed at once. Here, we integrate ideas from information theory, cognitive science,and neuroscience to offer a unified account of why processing is often so limited. We arguethat this reflects a fundamental tradeoff between generalization—how effectively existingrepresentations can be used in novel settings—and how many distinct representations canbe processed in parallel. Representations that best promote strong forms of generalization— a characteristically human cognitive strength — come at the expense of surprisinglystrict limits in the number of items that can be processed at once, an equally characteristichuman weakness. We refer to this as the “curse of generalization.” We formulate this first ininformation-theoretic terms, and then in process models, including a neural network modelof classic tasks used to demonstrate strict limits in human processing capacity. This tensionoffers a potential explanation for a range of phenomena — from performance on the tasks onwhich we focus, to representational learning and skill acquisition more broadly — as wellas the performance of modern machine learning architectures that exhibit generalizationcapabilities comparable to humans.

title: Assessing the Quality of AI Explanations of Atrial Fibrillation: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Google Gemini
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
598e2fa6d5c1d1ee8bb1eebc101a66353744cb13.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most common arrhythmias and is associated with multiple risk factors, including stroke and heart failure. Therefore, it is important that accurate and comprehensive educational resources on AF are available. Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms such as Google Gemini and ChatGPT are emerging tools for medical education. To our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the quality of these platforms for AF education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pilot study aimed to (1) assess the quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini explanations of AF and its treatment, (2) compare responses from both platforms, and (3) analyze differences in interpretation between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prompt “Explain atrial fibrillation and how to treat it to a patient” was entered into both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The responses, along with a survey created in Google Forms, were sent out to potential participants between September and October 2024. The survey questions were derived from the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials and DISCERN criteria. Each survey question was multiple choice and rated on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated strong disagreement and 5 indicated strong agreement. Averages of each answer from the survey were calculated and compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The survey was completed by 28 participants, including cardiologists and cardiology fellows and 17 nonmedical professionals (college graduates not employed in the medical field). No significant overall quality differences were observed between ChatGPT and Google Gemini. When comparing participant groups, cardiologists rated AI-generated responses higher than nonmedical professionals for perceived bias (mean 3.82 vs mean 4.33; P=.04) and for explaining consequences of no treatment (mean 2.85 vs mean 1.86; P=.005). In contrast, nonmedical professionals rated structural and organizational features more favorably than cardiologists, including visual cues (mean 3.97 vs mean 2.48; P<.001), informative headers (mean 4.77 vs mean 3.95; P=.001), concise sections (mean 4.71 vs mean 4.29; P=.04), identifiable patient actions (mean 4.21 vs mean 3.19; P=.04), and references to additional resources (mean 2.65 vs mean 1.71; P=.006).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The comparable quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini suggests that both are viable for AF education. Differences in ratings of organizational features versus perceptions of bias and consequences of no treatment highlight a disconnect between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals. To optimize clinical application, cardiologists should evaluate both comprehensiveness and clarity of AI-generated responses. This serves as a pilot study, and future research should focus on longitudinal studies of AI-generated responses and their effects on clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery, Endobariatrics, and AI - How AI is Contributing to Surgery and Endoscopy
Synthesis of critical-element-bearing olivine and pyroxene
container-title: American Mineralogist
fa36ab96a69bd4806df9e17391eab27f6b704817.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nickel (Ni) and cobalt (Co) are critical elements necessary for the transition to carbon-free energy generation. Increasing global demand for these elements requires new sources to be found. Both Ni and Co are found in low concentrations in mafic and ultramafic silicate minerals. To systematically understand the partitioning behavior of these elements in silicate minerals and to provide starting materials for experiments, we synthesized forsterite and enstatite with Ni and Co contents between 1.2 and 8.6 wt%. We find that &gt;95% purity syntheses of large batches (tens of grams) of both minerals are possible and that purity decreases with increasing Ni or Co dopant levels in enstatite syntheses. Impurities in forsterite syntheses include cristobalite and enstatite, while impurities in enstatite syntheses include cristobalite and forsterite. Partitioning of Ni and Co dopants favors forsterite over enstatite, with a more pronounced effect observed in Ni than Co. The doped minerals serve as starting materials for experiments that seek to extract critical elements from ultramafic and mafic rocks, in which the primary carriers of Ni and Co are olivine and pyroxene.</jats:p>

title: Assessing the Effectiveness, Engagement, and Acceptability of a Smartwatch Healthy Lifestyle Intervention for Cognitive Enhancement in Healthy Adults: Mixed Methods Electroencephalography Protocol
container-title: JMIR Research Protocols
7e6b65fd0eceaed8ad891218da9c81d3f193d863.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Wearable technologies are rapidly transforming the health care landscape by enabling the tracking of real-time physiological and behavioral data used in healthy lifestyle interventions. Despite their widespread adoption in the consumer market, scientific validation of their impact on the brain remains limited, and factors influencing effects on cognition and adherence are not fully understood. This gap is critical, as consumers, health care providers, and researchers depend on these data to unlock the potential of wearables for cognitive support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We aim to assess the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of a commercially available smartwatch healthy lifestyle intervention on cognitive enhancement in healthy adults, using a convergent parallel mixed methods design. We seek to provide a comprehensive, replicable methodological framework to evaluate wearable technology interventions targeting cognitive enhancement in healthy adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years with a sedentary lifestyle (N=72) interested in participating in a healthy lifestyle intervention will be recruited in the Vancouver Metropolitan Area, BC, Canada. Participants will be randomly assigned into an intervention group using an Apple Watch or a control group following standard physical activity guidelines without an Apple Watch for a period of 4 weeks. Effectiveness will be evaluated through (1) cognitive function (primary outcome)—executive function, specifically inhibitory control, via electroencephalogram-based event-related potentials (N2/P3) during a go/no-go task; (2) resting-state brain activity via electroencephalogram spectral power; (3) behavioral performance (reaction time and accuracy); (4) perceived health (36-item Short Form Health Survey); and (5) qualitative analysis of factors affecting the intervention’s effectiveness. Engagement will be assessed through goal completion metrics and qualitative analysis of barriers, facilitators, and usage patterns. Acceptability will be assessed through System Usability Scale scores and qualitative analysis of factors affecting usability, satisfaction, and user preferences. This design integrates assessments before, during, and after intervention. Qualitative assessments will include weekly check-ins and semistructured interviews to obtain a comprehensive understanding of factors influencing the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of the intervention. Exploratory outcomes include descriptions of possible interactions between the 3 constructs and comparison of smartwatch-tracked vs self-reported goal completion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study received funding from the AGE-WELL Network Centres of Excellence (April 2020-March 2023) and was approved by the Simon Fraser University Research Ethics Board. Enrollment for the study is ongoing. As of October 2026, data have been collected from 48 participants and are currently being processed and analyzed. The first results are expected to be published in 2027.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study outlines a foundational framework for evaluating the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of wearable health interventions targeting cognitive enhancement in healthy adults. Furthermore, our mixed methods approach with randomized controlled comparison is expected to inform the design and development of effective, engaging, and friendly wearable brain health technologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Thinking About Going to War in Iraq
container-title: Inside the George W. Bush White House
3b4d40256679f9af49eb8486514a8fd781ebb74e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>President Bush’s decision to invade Iraq—what State Department official Richard Haass described as a “war of choice” rather than a “war of necessity”—will probably be recalled in history as the most prominent item in Bush’s legacy. This chapter examines what Bush was thinking about Iraq before 9/11, and how those attacks altered the course of the administration on dealing with that country. The official policy of the US government since Bill Clinton’s second term had been to remove Saddam Hussein from power, but there was no consensus about how vigorously to pursue that aim. A sense of urgency increased dramatically after 9/11, when Bush was tugged in multiple directions, including by some in the Defense Department who thought Iraq should be their first target. For a time, Bush held them at bay. But once the invasion of Afghanistan was completed with relative ease, attention turned abruptly to Iraq.</jats:p>

title: Towards Realistic Project-Level Code Generation via Multi-Agent Collaboration and Semantic Architecture Modeling
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
2e98affb75fe6b1c9fa0a80bf39cb6bb48af6b14.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in automated code generation. In real-world software engineering, the growing demand for rapid iteration and continuous delivery underscores the importance of project-level code generation, where LLMs are expected to generate complete software projects directly from complex user requirements. This task, however, presents greater challenges due to larger input scales, multi-modal information, and the need for holistic architectural reasoning. Although existing studies have made initial explorations, they still face key limitations, including unrealistic datasets and unreliable evaluation metrics that fail to reflect real-world complexity, the semantic gap between human-written requirements and machine-interpretable structures, and difficulties in managing hierarchical dependencies and maintaining quality throughout the generation process. To address these limitations, we first introduce
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , a project-level code generation dataset built from 18 real-world repositories with 12.7 files and 2,388.6 lines of code per task on average, supplemented with documentation and executable test cases for automatic evaluation. We further propose
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    , a multi-agent framework that decomposes projects into architecture design, skeleton generation, and code filling stages with iterative refinement and memory-based context management. Within this framework, we introduce the Semantic Software Architecture Tree, a structured and semantically rich representation that effectively bridges user requirements and source code implementation. Experiments show that
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    achieves state-of-the-art performance, passing 52/124 test cases on the small-scale project-level code generation dataset DevBench, a 57% improvement over the baseline approaches, and 310 test cases on
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , representing an improvement of roughly tenfold compared to the baselines.
                  </jats:p>

title: Comparative Autism Research Effectiveness (CARE): Engaging the Neurodiversity Paradigm
container-title: Journal of Critical Study of Communication and Disability
f8c51d6ded3e45d32c9b5508f31f0d9273dcf153.abstract: <jats:p>Autism is a disability that is troubled by access to appropriate, education, medical, and health care. The grant Comparative Autism Research Effectiveness connected autistics, parents, and caregivers, researchers, and clinicians to assess current autism research and determine areas for improvement. Everyone came together for an online two-day conference along with participating in four follow-up calls. Four major themes emerged consisting of: (a) Consent, Participation, and Representation; (b) Language and Ethics; (c) Neurodiversity Paradigm and Autistic Inclusion; and, (d) Quality of Life and Trauma. Five top sub-themes included: (a) Neuro-affirming, gender affirming and trauma informed research; (b) Autistic inclusion in all aspects; (c) Moving away from a rigid medical model; (d) Embracing the Neurodiversity paradigm; and, (e) Moving towards neuroscience and away from behaviorism such as Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA). Autistics must be included in all aspects of research. Embracing neurodiversity and autistic neurodivergent-affirming care were predominant outcomes. </jats:p>

title: Power and Ideology in a Social Skills Training Curriculum for Autistic Teens: A Critical Discourse Analysis
container-title: Journal of Critical Study of Communication and Disability
cca146ebec0db21097db30e808eb2088df5adb08.abstract: <jats:p>Autistic youth often have difficulties navigating social spaces. Social skills training (SST) programs have been developed to improve their social competence. By applying Fairclough’s (1989) critical discourse analysis (CDA) in addition to neurodiversity frameworks, this paper aims to unpack power and ideology in a popular SST curriculum for autistic youth. Detailed analysis led to three findings. First, the curriculum authors’ discursive moves reveal their conceptualization of social appropriateness as non-negotiable facts and their ableist assumptions about autistic teens. Second, the authors constructed hierarchical relationships between the authors, therapists, and autistic teens through scripted lessons and varying sentence types. Third, the authors’ evaluative language revealed the manufacture of therapists’ and autistic teens' consent to the prescribed rules and subjected teens to constant evaluation. In conclusion, the manual discourses manifest neuronormative power and ableist ideologies that ultimately seek to correct autistic teens’ social practices.</jats:p>

title: La epistemología feminista como proyecto crítico y transformador del conocimiento
Feminist Epistemology as a Critical and Transformative Project of Knowledge
A EPISTEMOLOGIA FEMINISTA COMO PROJETO CRÍTICO E TRANSFORMADOR DO CONHECIMENTO
container-title: Análisis Filosófico
39dbf4074c1cca3d396ded84cacb3c2e6fd618a5.abstract: <jats:p>El objetivo de este trabajo es analizar la obra colectiva Epistemología feminista (2024), compilada por Danila Suárez Tomé, Laura F. Belli y Agostina Mileo, destacando su relevancia teórica, política y pedagógica. El libro muestra cómo la epistemología feminista pasó de una posición marginal a consolidarse como un campo plural, interdisciplinario, que critica las nociones tradicionales de objetividad, neutralidad y sujeto epistémico. A lo largo de dos partes, la obra articula debates teóricos —como los conocimientos situados, la teoría del punto de vista, la objetividad fuerte, la injusticia y la ignorancia epistémicas— con estudios de caso en ámbitos como la ciencia, la salud, la bioética, la inteligencia artificial y las políticas públicas. El volumen subraya que el conocimiento es una práctica social situada, atravesada por relaciones de poder, y defiende que la epistemología feminista no es anticientífica, sino una herramienta para construir una ciencia más democrática, inclusiva y responsable, capaz de visibilizar saberes históricamente excluidos y proponer alternativas transformadoras.</jats:p>

title: AI-Generated Exposure Hierarchies for Body Dysmorphic Disorder: Proof-of-Concept Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
475970c23de59b336f5f102fda0e80aa46b47e4e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is a chronic, impairing condition for which cognitive behavioral therapy, including exposure and response prevention (ERP), is the first-line treatment, but few clinicians are trained in BDD-specific ERP. Constructing personalized exposure hierarchies is time-intensive and requires clinical expertise, particularly for patients with absent insight who may hold appearance beliefs with delusional conviction. Generative AI (GenAI)–powered chatbots, such as ChatGPT, have shown utility for clinical content, but their capacity to produce safe, appropriate ERP hierarchies for BDD has not been examined.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the feasibility of using ChatGPT (GPT-5) to generate ERP hierarchies for BDD, assessed the influence of clinical and demographic characteristics on output quality, benchmarked AI-generated hierarchies against those created by doctoral-level BDD specialists, and tested whether blinded experts could distinguish AI-generated from expert-generated hierarchies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated 10-item graded exposure hierarchies for 72 simulated vignettes that varied by body area, insight level (good, limited, or absent), symptom specificity, age, and gender. Expert clinicians independently generated hierarchies for a subset of 18 vignettes. Two researchers rated all GPT-5 hierarchies for task completion and information integration. Three BDD expert clinicians, blinded to the hierarchy source (expert vs GPT-5), rated all 90 hierarchies for relevance, specificity, variability, safety, and overall quality. After unblinding, raters attempted to identify the AI-generated hierarchy in the 18 matched pairs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      GPT-5 generated complete hierarchies for 69 of 72 (95.8%) vignettes. Blinded experts rated GPT-5 hierarchies highly across all dimensions (mean scores ranging from 4.39, SD 0.26 to 4.90, SD 0.16 out of 5), with no significant differences from expert-generated hierarchies except for variability, where experts scored modestly higher (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.24). After unblinding, raters correctly identified AI-generated hierarchies only 31.5% (17/54) of the time, significantly below chance (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.009); this below-chance result was mostly due to one rater, and no rater performed above chance. Insight level was the most consistent predictor of quality: absent-insight hierarchies received significantly lower safety (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.73) and overall quality ratings (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.01;
                      <jats:italic>r</jats:italic>
                      =0.43). This pattern was not unique to GPT-5; safety ratings for expert-generated hierarchies also declined significantly by insight level (
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.03). Miscalibration of exposure difficulty, particularly for low- and absent-insight cases, was the most common rater concern (30/43, 69.8% comments), disproportionately directed at GPT-5 hierarchies.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GPT-5 generated ERP hierarchies for BDD that blinded experts rated as comparable to clinician-created hierarchies and could not reliably distinguish them from clinician-created hierarchies. However, hierarchies for patients with absent insight received lower safety and quality ratings from both AI and expert sources, and qualitative comments suggested AI-generated hierarchies were less well calibrated to delusional-level presentations. GenAI thus shows promise as a clinician-facing aid for ERP hierarchy generation, but these findings underscore the need for clinician oversight, especially for patients with delusional conviction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: SAI: Virtualizing Shared Memory of GPU for AI workload acceleration
container-title: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems
c8fa29b0323351e1659db262fc936958ed20d580.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    AI workloads increasingly demand high parallelism and efficient on-chip memory utilization on modern GPUs. However, the limited capacity of shared memory often constrains thread-level parallelism, while portions of the L2 cache remain underutilized. In this work, we propose
                    <jats:bold>SAI</jats:bold>
                    , a mechanism that virtualizes shared memory into the L2 cache to improve GPU performance for AI applications. SAI dynamically activates virtualization based on runtime resource usage, enabling additional CTAs with minimal architectural modifications. We further introduce an L2 cache management strategy that integrates associativity-based virtual page allocation and a replacement information table, reducing page-swapping overhead while preserving L2 cache performance. Experimental results demonstrate that SAI achieves an 18.6% performance improvement over the baseline design and outperforms SMILE-opt, our reproduced state-of-the-art baseline, by 8.8%. Moreover, SAI captures 60.2% of the performance gain delivered by the idealized Double SMEM design while reducing energy consumption to 87.7% of the baseline. These results highlight the effectiveness of SAI in enhancing thread-level parallelism and optimizing on-chip memory for AI workloads.
                  </jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Early Detection of Epidemic Threats in a Resource-Constrained Health System: Implementation Research from Lebanon
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
94bf395e649f9c13344c021277ab854ad6c98be5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Global South countries face heightened infectious disease risks compounded by fragmented surveillance systems and resource constraints. Lebanon’s health system crisis and recurrent outbreaks highlight the urgent need for new approaches to epidemic and pandemic preparedness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To describe the design, implementation process, and early implementation findings of an artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled early warning system (AI-EWS) that automates detection of epidemiologically relevant events using laboratory data in Lebanon, with emphasis on feasibility, workflow integration, stakeholder engagement, and implementation learnings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We applied an implementation research approach to co-design and validate an AI-EWS prototype integrated within a university hospital laboratory. The system incorporates a hybrid statistical and machine learning analytic pipeline and a real-time dashboard for detecting epidemic events across multiple pathogens using routine laboratory information systems (LIS) data. The system was developed in collaboration with the Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) to support future national adoption.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The project produced a structured framework for pathogen selection, rule development, dataset creation, and platform co-design with clinical and epidemiological experts, medical informatics professionals, MoPH experts, and technical specialists. Early implementation observations indicate operational feasibility within existing infrastructure, strong stakeholder engagement, and trust-building around AI-enabled surveillance through participatory design and responsible-AI governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AI-enabled laboratory surveillance is a viable and scalable approach to strengthening epidemic preparedness in low-resource health systems when grounded in implementation science and responsible AI, and when explicitly aligned with local workflows and national policy priorities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Bayesian Forecasting as the Analytical Core of an AI-Assisted Early Warning System for Dengue Outbreaks during the 2023 Epidemic: Implementation and Emergency Management in a Dominican Pediatric Hospital
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
056417fa3dbad64347775b6e5020ffb82cf01df1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Dengue remains a major cause of pediatric morbidity in the Dominican Republic, with increasingly intense epidemic cycles. Advances in statistical modeling, probabilistic forecasting, and AI-assisted digital health systems offer new opportunities to enhance early warning capabilities and strengthen hospital preparedness. This study evaluated a Bayesian negative binomial regression forecasting model as the analytical core of an AI-assisted early warning system (EWS) for predicting weekly dengue cases nationwide, using strict out-of-sample validation during the 2023 epidemic and applying its outputs operationally in a high-demand pediatric hospital. National surveillance data (PLISA/PAHO), hospital records from the Dr. Hugo Mendoza Pediatric Hospital (HPHM), and climatic and satellite indicators (NOAA, MODIS) for 2014–2024 were integrated. The model incorporated climatically plausible lags, harmonic seasonality, two vegetation indices (NDVI_lag4 and EVI_lag4), a long-term spline trend, and weakly informative priors, achieving excellent convergence (Rhat = 1.00). Climatic and environmental predictors exhibited small and uncertain effects, whereas the temporal spline accounted for most long-term epidemic variability. In the 2023 national validation, the model captured the broad epidemic trajectory and improved RMSE and MAE compared with the historical seasonal baseline (RMSE = 783.3; MAE = 423.4; MAPE = 80.2%), although proportional accuracy remained limited during abrupt epidemic acceleration. The national model also captured ascending-phase signals that were temporally aligned with the HPHM hospital outbreak, including its sharp rise during epidemiological weeks 36–40. These outputs were used alongside routine surveillance and hospital indicators to support operational situational awareness, capacity planning, patient-flow reorganization, strengthened triage, and emergency preparedness during the epidemic. The model demonstrated temporal signal detection and operational relevance, positioning Bayesian probabilistic forecasting, embedded within an AI-assisted digital health workflow, as a useful analytical component for epidemic monitoring and hospital preparedness, subject to limitations in peak magnitude calibration and proportional accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Toward Human-Centered Pedagogy in the Age of Generative AI Among Higher Education Educators: Qualitative Phenomenological Study
container-title: JMIR Medical Education
46248c918f688c3c5f2cc8bb261f150c45f4e9cf.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Generative AI (GenAI) expands possibilities for content generation, feedback, personalization, and instructional support in higher education. Its growing use also challenges established assumptions about teaching, assessment, professional expertise, academic integrity, and educational responsibility. Although research has examined technology adoption and AI competencies, less is known about how educators experience and interpret the pedagogical transformation associated with GenAI in everyday teaching.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study explored how higher education educators experience GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation, focusing on pedagogical practices, professional roles and expertise, educator agency, human-AI relationships, and associated opportunities and tensions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative phenomenological inquiry involved 23 educators from 3 Palestinian universities. Purposive maximum-variation sampling sought variation in academic rank, discipline, teaching experience, and experience with AI tools. Individual semistructured, in-depth interviews were conducted from March to April 2026, audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and returned to participants for review. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis informed by phenomenology. Initial coding was inductive and grounded in participants’ accounts; human-centered AI and sociomateriality subsequently informed interpretation as sensitizing concepts. Themes were developed through iterative comparison of transcripts, analytic memos, and alternative interpretations. Informational sufficiency was observed after approximately 20 interviews, with 3 additional interviews used to examine the developing thematic structure.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis generated 8 interconnected themes. Educators described a shift from content transmission toward mediation, inquiry, reflective learning, creative exploration, and process-oriented assessment. Professional expertise increasingly centered on facilitation, pedagogical design, contextual interpretation, ethical guidance, and evaluation of AI-generated content. Human-AI collaboration involved bounded and integrated configurations, with humans retaining responsibility for judgment and educational consequences. Educator agency appeared through decisions about AI participation, independent student reasoning, and the boundaries of human expertise. Credibility, bias, authorship, authenticity, and academic integrity became embedded as pedagogical concerns. Participants valued opportunities for creativity, personalization, flexibility, and instructional support while expressing concerns about dependence, reduced intellectual effort, and weakened human connection.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>GenAI-mediated pedagogical transformation depends on educators’ alignment of AI use with learning purposes, the allocation of responsibilities, and the preservation of ethical accountability and meaningful relationships. The resulting human-centered pedagogy framework positions pedagogical intentionality, contextual judgment, negotiated agency, and relational presence as central to responsible integration. Universities should complement technical training and institutional policies with support for pedagogical design, critical evaluation, process-oriented assessment, and ethical reasoning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
