The positive relationship between adaptation outcomes and AI trust is supported by PLS-SEM, with the cognitive load change as a mediator and the organisational learning orientation as a moderator, the most significant institutional factor influencing adaptation outcomes. The chapter suggests embedding metacognition and AI literacy in workforce governance, institutional reflection in HR and L&D processes, and complementarity guardrails. For practical governance tools for adopting responsible AI in higher education, a validated diagnostic instrument and a Human-AI Capability Convergence Model are provided.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy–Based Digital Interventions for Illicit Substance Use Disorders: Scoping Review of Intervention Design, Efficacy Indicators, and Methodological Gaps
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
9d1858cff34c91ccfc45c7d996e799804ca90d99.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Illicit substance use disorders (SUDs) are escalating globally; yet, social stigma and legal barriers restrict access to conventional treatment, and existing research remains skewed toward alcohol and nicotine. Digital interventions incorporating cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) offer a discreet, scalable alternative.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review maps how CBT-based digital interventions for illicit SUDs are designed and delivered across platforms, identifying their theoretical frameworks, functional components, outcome indicators, and reported methodological limitations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) scoping review methodology and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews). Six databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, APA PsycINFO, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library, and CINAHL) were searched from inception to June 28, 2026, without language, date, or study design limits, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching (July 3, 2026). Eligible studies were empirical primary studies quantitatively evaluating digital interventions incorporating CBT for illicit or nonprescribed substance use; alcohol- or nicotine-only populations were excluded. Three reviewers independently screened and charted all studies, with disagreements resolved by consensus or adjudication. Data were synthesized narratively, with tables, figures, and an evidence gap map.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifty-six studies published between 2008 and 2026, drawn from 47 distinct participant samples, met the eligibility criteria. Most were conducted in North America (40/56, 71.4%) and used randomized controlled designs (39/56, 69.6%). Polysubstance-using populations were most frequently targeted (32/56, 57.1%), followed by cannabis (13/56, 23.2%), opioids (6/56, 10.7%), and stimulants (5/56, 8.9%). Interventions were delivered mainly via web (24/56, 42.9%) or app (24/56, 42.9%) platforms, and most (49/56, 87.5%) were grounded in traditional CBT, most often combined with contingency management (18/56, 32.1%) or motivational interviewing (17/56, 30.4%). Core functional components included therapeutic intervention (55/56, 98.2%), self-tracking and notification (25/56, 44.6%), reward (24/56, 42.9%), and support and feedback (21/56, 37.5%). Primary outcomes focused on substance use and abstinence (41/56, 73.2%), retention/feasibility (16/56, 28.6%), and mental health status or coping skills (14/56, 25%). Author-reported limitations were predominantly participant-level (52/56, 92.9%), measurement-level (43/56, 76.8%), study-level (34/56, 60.7%), and intervention-level (25/56, 44.6%) domains.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Unlike previous reviews confined to a single substance or delivery platform, this review is innovative in mapping CBT-based digital interventions across the full spectrum of illicit substances, including polysubstance use, and in linking their functional components to intended therapeutic mechanisms. It thereby contributes to the development of these technologies and, by synthesizing author-reported limitations, proposes methodological improvements for their future evaluation. At present, CBT-based digital interventions are best positioned as adjuncts that extend the reach and continuity of existing addiction care rather than as stand-alone substitutes for it; substance-specific customization, objective outcome measures, and modular trial designs are needed to establish them as scalable clinical tools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Cognitive Digital Twins and Blockchain Ecosystems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Next-Generation Supply Chain Management in the Industrial Metaverse
800c4603905b0b481af418f93c27b335627b538c.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter develops an architecture for combining cognitive digital twins with blockchain ecosystems to deliver predictive business intelligence in the industrial metaverse. It argues that digital-twin initiatives create value only when operational telemetry, semantic context, decision models, and human governance are connected through trusted data-sharing and executable coordination mechanisms. Drawing on research in digital twins, industrial metaverse design, blockchain-enabled provenance, smart contracts, human-centric manufacturing, and explainable AI, the chapter proposes a layered reference architecture, performance metrics, implementation logic, and governance controls. It also examines persistent challenges, including semantic fragmentation, model drift, latency, privacy, interoperability, energy cost, and the oracle problem. The chapter concludes with design recommendations and a research agenda for resilient, trustworthy, and economically useful industrial intelligence systems across networked industrial-metaverse platforms and ecosystems.</jats:p>

title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
Beyond Recognition
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
8d55c03606f397dfebd690ec5704784da2344f3c.abstract: <jats:p>Current e-learning systems are still not well-suited to learn in real-time as individuals' emotional and cognitive state. The chapter presents AIALE (Affective Intelligence Adaptive Learning Engine), a multimodal system capable of embedding facial coding, bio signals, keystroke dynamics and eye-tracking in a single pipeline and with sub-500ms inference latency. The AIALE's three-tier architecture consists of a deep learning-based effect inference, a reinforcement learning-based curriculum control and a pedagogic intervention broker. AIALE was tested with 214 university students from four disciplines and led to statistically significant increases in knowledge gain (31% above that of a knowledge-adaptive baseline) as well as to an increase in engagement duration and a balance of cognitive load, compared to a knowledge-adaptive baseline and a non-adaptive control. An ablation analysis shows that the most significant affective dimensions for adaptive interventions' quality are confusion and cognitive load detection. The chapter also introduces five research gaps and explores emerging research avenues such as generative AI tutoring agents and explainable affective adaptation.</jats:p>

title: Camera-Based Deep Learning Framework for Real-Time Emotion-Aware Engagement Detection in E-Learning
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
10cfc4979912c42a01924f13bd2193ca5e197ab1.abstract: <jats:p>The explosive expansion of digital learning platforms has revolutionized the manner in which students access, consume, and interact with academic content. Sustaining high levels of engagement within online spaces, though, remains perhaps the most critical challenge facing higher education. Conventional methods of measuring engagement—e.g., tracking presence, post-session questionnaires, or physiological sensors—are intrusively burdensome, not very reliable, and less than ideal for widespread implementation. Technological developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning provide non-invasive means, notably via camera-based emotion detection systems that are able to track and decipher learner engagement real-time. This chapter suggests a human-focused deep learning approach that incorporates facial emotion detection with adaptive learning routes to boost learner engagement and mental growth in e-learning contexts.</jats:p>

title: Challenges and Ethical Considerations in Gamified and Cognitive Learning in Cybersecurity Education
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
fe7c56a27e63d56369910ade1fabf1dae4d33295.abstract: <jats:p>Gamified and cognitive learning in cybersecurity education is gaining popularity, but it brings its own set of challenges, particularly when it comes to ethics. Training through games can sharpen technical skills, yet there's always the risk of blurring the lines between ethical hacking and actual cybercrime. Some learners may be tempted to misuse their knowledge, especially if ethical considerations aren't woven into the experience from the start. Then there's the question of real-world readiness—does solving puzzles in a simulated environment translate to handling live cyber threats? Beyond that, data privacy is a concern. Gamified platforms track progress, but how much of that data should they collect, and who gets access? And let's not ignore the psychology behind game mechanics, does intense competition fuel motivation or push players toward reckless behavior? The key lies in balance. Industry and academia need to step in with clear ethical guidelines, ensuring that gamification encourages responsibility alongside skill-building. A well-designed system can use storytelling, role-playing, and collaborative challenges to reinforce ethical decision-making rather than just technical mastery. AI could play a role in adapting training to individuals, but it raises ethical dilemmas. Cybersecurity threats are constantly changing, so training must evolve too. Gamified education can be a powerful tool, but only if it's designed with ethics at its core.</jats:p>

title: Deep Learning Architectures for Real-Time Emotion and Engagement Detection in E-Learning Platforms
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
f9731fd32e93095cf320cc72899c5ae1486d338c.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of deep learning into e-learning environments has revolutionised the way learners interact with educational content. This study explores the design and implementation of deep learning architectures for real-time emotion and engagement detection in e-learning platforms. By leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and transformer-based models, the proposed framework captures multimodal data such as facial expressions, speech tone, eye movement, and physiological signals to assess learners' emotional states and engagement levels dynamically. The system provides adaptive feedback to instructors and personalised interventions to learners, enhancing cognitive growth and overall learning outcomes. The research also discusses the challenges of real-time processing, model interpretability, data privacy, and ethical considerations associated with emotion recognition technologies in education.</jats:p>

title: Deep Learning for Modern E-Learning Systems
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
9aaf4dfff445fa1aad16b80d1c5376fcd12ec6c4.abstract: <jats:p>Models that learn from users and content interact at scale. This chapter articulates the many uses of highly layered neural networks in personalization, applied feedback, and text, speech, code, image, and video assistance. The main model families are described: CNNs, RNNs / LSTMs, transformers, autoencoders, and other generative models; as are the approaches to training, optimizing, regularizing, and deploying models. Representation learning from unstructured data, adaptive pathways, engagement and emotion detection, and predicting performance and studying are learning outcomes that guide model choice. System elements include data gathering, analytics, model serving in-cloud or on-device, and scale. Intelligent tutoring, recommendation, auto-grading, and dialogue systems on modern platforms are current use cases. Trade-offs include privacy, sparse supervision, bias, lack of explainability, seamlessness to legacy systems, and computation cost. Real-world deployments, both successful and not, are the focus of the illustrative case studies. The chapter's focus is on core techniques and design choices to build the next generation of e-learning systems.</jats:p>

title: Deep Learning-Driven Emotion Recognition for Personalized and Adaptive E-Learning Systems
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
ce676f08ce46956bb22f53f59a27b6cbe5ec864b.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores how deep learning–based emotion recognition enhances student engagement and cognitive growth in e-learning environments. By leveraging CNN and LSTM architectures, the proposed framework detects learners' emotions from facial and behavioral cues in real time, enabling adaptive instructional responses. Through camera-based, non-invasive monitoring, emotions such as confusion, curiosity, or satisfaction are quantified to personalize learning experiences and improve retention. The chapter also discusses dataset selection, model design, and integration into Learning Management Systems (LMS). Case insights demonstrate how emotion-aware systems foster empathy, motivation, and inclusivity in digital education. Ethical considerations privacy, fairness, and explainability are addressed to ensure responsible AI deployment. The study establishes emotion recognition as a cornerstone for intelligent, adaptive, and human-centered e-learning ecosystems that align technology with emotional intelligence and pedagogical effectiveness.</jats:p>

title: How Gamification Mechanics Improve Cybersecurity Learning Retention
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
e507f4e7f41e686a6ea10856a0a000bbacf36594.abstract: <jats:p>Gamification taps into how the brain processes rewards, emotions, and repetition, making it a powerful tool for cybersecurity education. When learners engage with challenges that trigger dopamine release—like solving puzzles, earning achievements, or progressing through a story—retention improves. The way emotions shape memory also plays a role; high-stakes simulations and immersive storytelling make security concepts stick. Incorporating game mechanics, such as real-time feedback, narrative-driven exercises, and adaptive difficulty, strengthens learning. Capture the Flag competitions and VR-based training reinforce hands-on skills, while spaced repetition counters memory decay. More than just engagement, this approach helps reduce anxiety by creating a safe space for trial and error, building confidence without the fear of real-world consequences. As AI begins to refine personalized learning paths, cybersecurity training can adapt to individual strengths and weaknesses. Long-term, this shift could shape a more prepared, responsive workforce—one that learns through experience, not just theory. But with any gamified system, balance is key.</jats:p>

title: Natural Language Processing for Interactive Learning Experiences
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
987c3de7f795db1cc232a6a4b1b49390a428ce0f.abstract: <jats:p>Natural Language Processing (NLP) has become a core component for next generation e-learning ecosystems, especially in content delivery. It enables platforms to understand, respond and adapt to individual learners. With the rise of deep learning models especially transformer based architectures, NLP now offers state of the art capabilities for real-time interaction, personalized feedback, and adaptive learning pathways. This chapter examines NLP-driven systems powered by deep learning to enhance learner engagement, motivation, and cognitive development. It is developed by converting static educational materials into dynamic, conversational, and highly interactive experiences. The key ideas in this chapter includes understanding text, language models that can generate responses, intelligent tutoring systems, automatic grading, feedback that considers emotions, and learning that uses multiple types of media (such as text, audio, and images). Practical use cases and emerging research trends are highlighted. Ethical, pedagogical and technological challenges are also discussed.</jats:p>

title: Passive Learning to Active Engagement
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
eacaa5f4ae36bc7dc2909810ec0a52e6a7081ebd.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid evolution of digital technologies has transformed the educational landscape, challenging traditional passive learning models and emphasizing the need for active engagement in deep learning. Passive learning, characterized by one-way information delivery and limited learner interaction, often results in superficial comprehension and low retention. In contrast, active engagement leverages interactive digital tools, collaborative strategies, and learner-centered approaches to foster critical thinking, problem-solving, and meaningful knowledge construction. This chapter explores the theoretical underpinnings of passive and active learning, examines the pedagogical shift facilitated by digital technologies, and highlights effective strategies for promoting deep learning in contemporary educational environments. Case studies from diverse educational contexts illustrate how digital pedagogy can bridge the gap between passive reception and active participation, ultimately enhancing learner motivation, engagement, and long-term retention.</jats:p>

title: Real-Time Multimodal Engagement Detection in E-Learning
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
cc8c8875c98107da22dfb5309173f1535042c386.abstract: <jats:p>The transition from in-person classrooms to digital and hybrid modes of learning has created new opportunities but has also posed several serious problems for education. One of the most key problems is the measurement of student engagement. This chapter discusses the use of deep learning for multimodal engagement detection to analyze visual data, auditory data, and behavioral data. By combining these signals, the adaptive feedback loops can be built supporting the learning. This chapter presents artificial intelligence together with psychological theories of the motivation, attention, and cognitive load in order to design human-centered environments that help teachers to be more efficient. Ethical issues like privacy, consent, and bias are dealt with to make sure they are utilized in a responsible manner. The chapter includes case studies from India and also other parts of the globe, showing the opportunities and challenges. The design of the system is proposed as a framework including pipelines, and integration with learning platforms.</jats:p>

title: The Psychology of Deep Learning for Student Engagement and Cognitive Development
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
388c0f1038cc6f8828ff44b71c150147ada103bd.abstract: <jats:p>Against the background of deep learning for engagement and cognitive growth in e-learning, the purpose of this chapter is to discuss findings from a real-world case study implementation at a Higher Education Institution (HEI) in Namibia. Towards addressing the psychology of deep learning for student engagement and cognitive development by reconfiguring e-learning accessibility via mobile technologies, the main focus of the chapter will be on tools, platforms, and gaps, as well as challenges and limitations, related to e-learning ecosystems. Future research directions based on the findings will be presented in order to come to conclusions toward smarter, fairer, human-centered learning.</jats:p>

title: Simultaneous ChatGPT-4o outputs for type 2 diabetes pharmacotherapy: Accuracy, usefulness, and impact variability
container-title: American Journal of Health-System Pharmacy
2afb1c76481981db74c1126b818adcd30e496879.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The primary objective of the study was to determine how clinically accurate and useful ChatGPT-4o–generated outputs are when identical prompts are entered simultaneously in 3 independent ChatGPT sessions utilizing the same user-facing model. The secondary objective was to identify whether differences in outputs affect clinical outcomes (ie, impact variability).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five clinical prompts focusing on diabetes management and counseling were developed. Each clinical prompt was simultaneously inputted into 3 separate devices using ChatGPT-4o to generate outputs. Through a modified Delphi technique, 5 clinical pharmacy faculty members with expertise in diabetes management independently rated each ChatGPT-generated output for accuracy (poor, borderline, or good) usefulness (not useful, somewhat useful, or very useful) and impact variability (low, moderate, or high). After initial assessment, responses were collated and anonymously shared among the pharmacy faculty raters. The faculty members were invited to revise their evaluations based on collective feedback, then convened in a virtual panel with moderators to discuss evaluations and work towards consensus.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Consensus was achieved for all ChatGPT outputs. Accuracy ratings ranged from borderline to good. Two of the clinical prompts yielded outputs that received different accuracy ratings, which may have impacted variability. Usefulness ratings ranged from somewhat useful to very useful, with one clinical prompt yielding outputs that received different usefulness ratings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While ChatGPT-4o outputs were generally accurate and useful, limitations and inconsistencies were noted. Users should be aware simultaneously generated outputs across multiple devices using ChatGPT can vary in their accuracy and usefulness in diabetes management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: CogniPaz, an Ecologically Oriented Gamified mHealth Tool for Detecting Mild Cognitive Impairment: Prospective Cohort Diagnostic Accuracy Study
container-title: JMIR mHealth and uHealth
5e441833bc2d296fe5085af9f436bc7fe5119c70.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Discriminating mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from subjective cognitive decline (SCD), and healthy controls (HC) remains challenging. Digital tools may overcome paper-and-pencil screening’s limitations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and usability of CogniPaz (Daniel Blanco), an ecologically oriented, mobile health (mHealth), gamified cognitive assessment tool exploring memory and executive functions, in discriminating MCI (particularly amnestic phenotypes [aMCI]) from SCD, and HC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This prospective observational study recruited a convenience sample of consecutive patients with cognitive complaints and HC at La Paz University Hospital Cognitive Disorders Unit from April 2025 to January 2026. Demographic and clinical characteristics, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores were collected. An evaluator blinded to the MoCA scores oversaw the automated, self-administered CogniPaz assessment. Participants were classified into HC (no cognitive complaints, MoCA score≥26), SCD (cognitive complaints, MoCA score≥26), and MCI (cognitive complaints without functional impairment, MoCA score<26, subdivided into amnestic [aMCI] and nonamnestic phenotypes). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses using age-adjusted models, the DeLong test, and bootstrap validation evaluated diagnostic accuracy across groups. The correlation between MoCA and CogniPaz scores was assessed using Spearman rank correlation. Participants with available biomarker data underwent exploratory analysis of CogniPaz’s ability to detect biologically confirmed any-cause neurodegeneration (bND). Usability was tested using an ad hoc Likert questionnaire (1‐9 points).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The participants (n=84, 57.1% female; median age 72.0, IQR 62.5-77.0 years) included 27 HC, 17 with SCD, 22 with aMCI, and 18 with nonamnestic MCI. The aMCI group was older than the SCD group (age: median 76.5, IQR 70.8-78.8 vs median 59.0, IQR 50.0-69.0 years; Kruskal-Wallis/Dunn,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.003). CogniPaz scores correlated with MoCA scores (ρ
                      <jats:italic>=</jats:italic>
                      0.81, 95% CI 0.75‐0.89;
                      <jats:italic>P<</jats:italic>
                      .001). CogniPaz showed good concurrent accuracy, independently of age: MCI vs HC (area under the curve [AUC]=0.880, 95% CI 0.798‐0.961), MCI vs SCD (AUC=0.915, 95% CI 0.841‐0.990), aMCI vs HC (AUC=0.910, 95% CI 0.830‐0.990), and aMCI vs SCD (AUC=0.943, 95% CI 0.878‐1.000). At the provisional <28.5 cutoff point, sensitivity ranged from 85.0% (34/40, 95% CI 70.2‐94.3) to 90.9% (20/22, 95% CI 70.8‐98.9) and specificity from 74.1% (20/27, 95% CI 53.7‐88.9) to 82.4% (14/17, 95% CI 56.6‐96.2) across comparisons. CogniPaz suggested capacity to detect bND (AUC=0.810, 95% CI 0.661‐0.958), with potential incremental value over MoCA and age (odds ratio [OR]=0.78, 95% CI 0.60‐0.94;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02). Median administration time was 9.39 (IQR 7.53‐11.38) minutes with 100% (84/84) completion. User satisfaction was high (median score 8.4/9, IQR 7.9‐8.6; Cronbach α=0.84).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CogniPaz is an innovative, user-friendly mHealth tool that addresses classical cognitive screening tools’ limitations through a brief, multidomain, minimally supervised gamified format, with high patient acceptance. It correlates with MoCA scores, shows good concurrent capacity to differentiate MCI, particularly aMCI, from SCD and HC, and appears promising for identifying bND. Pending external longitudinal validation, these findings support CogniPaz as a candidate for early cognitive screening in primary care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Stories of the Pewenche people: memory of care and resurgence of mountain commons
container-title: Community Development Journal
a4cfbb24a4231dd8b1603b419ceb707f2821b0d3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This document presents 3 stories of the Pewenche people who inhabit the foothills of the Andes and the pewen (Araucaria araucana) forests to problematize commons from a decolonial perspective. First, the seasonal cycles of wintering, summering, and the harvesting of ngüillio (the seed of the pewen), which ensure the survival of herds while preserving the integrity of forests and pastures. Second, community-based tourism initiatives, which have strengthened the local economy and contributed to environmental stewardship. Third, the memory and reactivation of ancient trans-Andean trade routes, whose revitalization reinforces communal identity and territorial attachment. Given that the Pewenche community of Alto Biobío has faced historical and recent processes of dispossession and forced displacement, these experiences offer a valuable lens through which to reflect on the practices of commoning. They invite us to interrogate the imposed notions of property and territorial boundaries in the highlands, which restrict traditional mobility and customary cycles; to revalue community economies—rooted in gathering, herding, and tourism—as key strategies for the care and defense of the commons, and to raise critical questions about who has the right to use, care for, and relate to Pewementu, and from which ontological positions such claims are made.</jats:p>

title: Exploring ChatGPT-Assisted Qualitative Data: Comparing Human and AI-Assisted Coding Using Braun and Clarke’s Thematic Analysis
container-title: American Journal of Qualitative Research
d1da3462e4a00cf9a9e2a1ed853867d5195ec143.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en"><i>The use of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, has significantly expanded across academia and research in recent years. Of growing interest is AI’s potential role in qualitative research, especially in expediting tasks such as literature review and synthesis, data management and coding, and manuscript preparation, all while striving to maintain the rigor expected of qualitative inquiry. This paper explores the degree of alignment between AI-generated thematic analysis and a traditional, manual approach to analyzing focus group data and potential uses of AI in qualitative research. Using Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis framework, a publicly available focus group dataset was analyzed in three stages: (1) Data Familiarization, (2) Human-Led Thematic Analysis, and (3) AI-Generated Analysis using ChatGPT. The human coders followed all six phases of the framework prior to engaging with the AI, to prevent influence from AI-generated output. The comparison revealed partial overlap between the human and AI-generated categories, particularly at the level of broader categories and themes. However, ChatGPT’s analysis tended to reflect a more superficial reading of the data, lacking the interpretive depth and nuance demonstrated by the human coders. While AI tools like ChatGPT show potential for supporting certain aspects of qualitative analysis, this study highlights key limitations in their ability to fully replicate the complexity and contextual understanding that human-led analysis provides. Further exploration is needed to define appropriate and ethical roles for AI in qualitative research workflows.</i></jats:p>

title: Reconnoitring Yogic Peace of Mind and Transient Happiness With Their Perceived Psychological Correlates
container-title: The Neuroscience of Happiness
2a08909a0d86148aae4b34a85733003e4a4fe6d2.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter discusses yogic peace of mind as a complex, self-reported psychological construct and looks into its linkages with perceived cognition, emotional regulation, meditative consciousness, and well-being. The empirical part of the research is a pilot cross-sectional study conducted only using data collected via questionnaires; it did not include measurements of brain activity, neurotransmitter levels, the autonomic nervous system, or any other biological parameters. Consequently, all neurological hypotheses are discussed as interpretations based on existing neuroscience literature and not on the findings of this particular research. Some preliminary findings of factor, regression, and structural modeling analyses will be used to evaluate the proposed theoretical links between the concepts. There is evidence of correlations between long-term yogic practice, reported peace of mind, and positive psychological outcomes; however, there is no proof of causation or physiological changes. Further large-scale longitudinal studies are required to verify the hypothesis.</jats:p>

title: The application of an artificial intelligence–enhanced virtual reality cognitive behavioral therapy tool is feasible and acceptable in patients with inflammatory bowel disease: A multicenter mixed methods pilot study
container-title: Inflammatory Bowel Diseases
34e53c5af6594279fbcef7d176c277418b8c6c44.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) frequently experience anxiety, pain, and reduced quality of life. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is effective for anxiety, but access may be limited. We evaluated the feasibility and explored the potential clinical impact of an artificial intelligence–powered virtual reality CBT-based application (XAIA [eXtended Reality Artificially Intelligent Ally]) in patients with IBD.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This was a multicenter, mixed-methods pilot study recruiting adults with IBD from the University of Chicago and Cedars-Sinai medical centers. Participants completed a single 30-minute session with the XAIA conversational avatar. Pain and anxiety were measured before and after the session using a visual analog pain scale and State–Trait Anxiety Inventory, respectively. Semi-structured interviews were conducted after the session to assess acceptability. Quantitative analysis was completed using paired t tests, and interview transcripts underwent thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Thirty-four participants (median age 34 years, 71% women, 59% with Crohn’s disease) participated in this study. Qualitative analysis revealed high acceptability, with participants reporting feelings of safety, validation, and improved coping. Participants valued the immersive environment, conversational avatar, and ability to discuss sensitive topics without judgment. As an exploratory outcome, participants reported a statistically significant improvement in pain (−0.46; P = .011) and anxiety (−10.65; P &lt; .001) immediately following a single session.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A single artificial intelligence–driven virtual reality CBT-based session in patients with IBD was feasible and well accepted and demonstrated preliminary evidence for acute reductions in pain and anxiety scores. Immersive digital behavioral health interventions may represent a scalable adjunct to traditional mental health support among adults with IBD.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Immersive Virtual Reality Cognitive Stimulation for Delirium Prevention in Older Surgical Intensive Care Unit Patients With Cognitive Impairment: Protocol for a 3-Arm Randomized Pilot Trial
container-title: JMIR Research Protocols
6a0305024bfe7ca8c2a7ec25512ab1521c9d9887.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Postoperative delirium is common among older adults after major surgery, especially those with cognitive impairment, and is associated with prolonged hospitalization, functional decline, mortality, and subsequent cognitive deterioration. Nonpharmacologic delirium-prevention strategies are recommended but are difficult to deliver reliably in high-acuity environments because they require repeated staff-intensive interactions, consistent patient engagement, and integration into complex intensive care unit (ICU) workflows.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to evaluate the feasibility, usability, safety, acceptance, and adherence of ReCognitionVR 2.0, an immersive virtual reality (VR)–based cognitive stimulation intervention designed for older surgical ICU patients with mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This is a single-center, 3-arm, parallel-group randomized pilot trial. Ninety adults aged 65 years or older undergoing major surgery with expected postoperative ICU admission and Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores of 15 to 24 will be randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to ReCognitionVR 2.0 cognitive stimulation, passive VR control exposure, or standard-of-care nurse-led reality orientation. VR sessions will be delivered once daily for up to 20 minutes on postoperative days 1 through 3 when participants are calm and alert. The primary outcomes are feasibility metrics, including recruitment, outcome completion, safety and tolerability, usability, acceptance, and adherence. Secondary outcomes estimate preliminary changes in attention and executive function using the Months Backward Test and NIH Toolbox Flanker Inhibitory Control and Attention Test. Postoperative delirium incidence is an exploratory clinical outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study was funded in September 2025. Participant recruitment and data collection are currently ongoing. Preliminary data quality assessments and exploratory reviews of the collected data are underway. Formal statistical analyses of the trial outcomes will be conducted after participant enrollment is completed and the study database has been finalized and locked. As of July 29, 2026, we had enrolled 18 participants. Early operational experience informed the refinement of exploratory VR performance metrics and the documentation of protocol deviations. Following an oxygen-connection near miss, we added a preintervention oxygen/readiness checklist as an operational safety safeguard. Enrollment of 90 participants is projected to be completed in 2027 if the current recruitment pace is sustained. Results are expected to be published in winter 2027.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This protocol will generate data on feasibility, safety, usability, adherence, digital performance, cognitive assessment, and delirium measurement, all needed to optimize ReCognitionVR 2.0 and to design a future multicenter efficacy trial of VR-enabled delirium prevention in critical care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Should quantum physics be approached with mathematical formalism in school? Effects of instructional approach on functional understanding under cognitive and affective controls
container-title: Physical Review Physics Education Research
6493f05b70eb976685bab6227f1a5b655fc3ff28.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Evidence from physics education research suggests that the introduction of mathematical formalism in quantum physics instruction can support the development of students’ conceptual understanding, particularly by promoting functional ways of reasoning about quantum phenomena. However, empirical findings on the effectiveness of such approaches at the secondary school level remain inconclusive, and little is known about the extent to which learning outcomes are shaped by instructional design as opposed to learners’ affective and cognitive characteristics. This study addresses this gap by investigating the relative influence of instructional approach on students’ understanding of single-photon states, while controlling for prior knowledge, cognitive load, situational interest, and physics self-concept. A quasiexperimental pre-post design was implemented with
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:mi>N</a:mi>
                      <a:mo>=</a:mo>
                      <a:mn>172</a:mn>
                    </a:math>
                    upper secondary students, comparing a qualitative instructional condition with an approach supplemented by a reduced Dirac formalism. Learning outcomes were assessed using the framework of Functional Fidelity and Fidelity of Gestalt. A multivariate analysis of covariance, followed by univariate analyses of covariance, was conducted to examine the contributions of instructional and learner-related variables. The findings indicate that affective variables emerge as strong predictors of functional understanding and suggest that learning in quantum physics is driven less by instructional format than by learners’ affective and cognitive prerequisites. In particular, fostering interest appears to be a key mechanism for supporting the development of functional understanding. The results highlight the importance of integrating affective dimensions into instructional design and provide a basis for future research on the interaction between instructional approaches and learner characteristics in quantum physics education.
                  </jats:p>

title: Application of Digital Health Interventions for Cognitive Management in Children With Cancer: Scoping Review
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
488230a323f4a1db95fece744265b1e2765b04ec.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Advances in the diagnosis and treatment of childhood cancer have substantially improved survival, resulting in a growing population of survivors of childhood cancer who may experience long-term treatment-related sequelae. Cognitive late effects are an important long-term consequence of childhood cancer and can affect cognitive functioning, psychosocial well-being, and quality of life. Digital health interventions offer accessible and flexible approaches to managing cognitive difficulties among children with cancer. However, the existing evidence has not yet been comprehensively synthesized.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to map and synthesize the existing evidence on digital health interventions for cognitive management among children with cancer; characterize intervention modalities, delivery approaches, and functional components; and identify evidence gaps and priorities for future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Arksey and O’Malley framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews) checklist. Six academic databases, including PubMed, Embase (Ovid), CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, were systematically searched for relevant studies published between January 2010 and August 2026. Eligibility criteria were developed using the population-concept-context framework. Two reviewers independently performed study screening and data extraction. The methodological quality of included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Screening was performed independently at the title/abstract and full-text stages, with disagreements resolved through discussion and, when necessary, consultation with a third reviewer. Descriptive statistics and thematic content analysis were used to synthesize the findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 5371 records were identified through the literature search. Following screening, 19 publications representing 14 independent study samples and involving 566 children with cancer were included. Four digital health modalities were identified: computer-based interventions, internet-based interventions, mobile apps, and neurofeedback training. Computer-based interventions were the predominant modality. Across these modalities, working memory and attention were the most frequently targeted cognitive domains, while feasibility, acceptability, and adherence were the most commonly assessed implementation-related outcomes. However, relatively few interventions incorporated coach support, telephone-based communication, or educational components, and none evaluated economic outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Although digital health interventions show promise for supporting cognitive function in children with cancer, substantial gaps remain in the current evidence. This scoping review mapped the field according to intervention modalities, delivery approaches, and functional components, rather than focusing solely on the efficacy of individual technologies. Future research should prioritize the development of multidimensional, personalized, and functionally integrated digital health interventions that combine cognitive training with supportive care, education, monitoring, and communication. Multicenter randomized controlled trials should subsequently evaluate these interventions using clinically meaningful outcomes, with comprehensive assessments of safety, adherence, implementation, and health economic outcomes to establish their effectiveness, feasibility, and sustainability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
bf7bc1447e7ed3caf087f04fb77606d4e98c71c2.abstract: <jats:p>While research on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and prompt literacy has expanded rapidly, an integrated framework explaining prompt-mediated learning remains underdeveloped. We introduce the Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding (PBCS) model, which conceptualizes prompts as regulatory mechanisms that coordinate cognitive, epistemic, and metacognitive processes during human–AI interaction. Building on cognitive scaffolding, distributed cognition, epistemic cognition, and prompt literacy, PBCS explains learning as a recursive coordination process in which human reasoning and AI-generated outputs are continuously refined. The model is operationalized through three interacting scaffolding dimensions and a functional prompt typology. Its explanatory scope is demonstrated across seminar-based learning, academic writing, collaborative learning, and research-oriented inquiry. We provide a theoretical foundation for understanding recursive human–AI knowledge construction.</jats:p>

title: Prompt Engineering as Distributed Cognition and Epistemic Infrastructure in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
d3ce7c75e5f8d37877d734c90b6dc48c96bd1c5b.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter theorizes prompt literacy as epistemic infrastructure in higher education, conceptualizing prompting as distributed cognition across learners, generative systems, artifacts, and disciplinary genres. It models prompting as a regulated workflow of specification, constraint-synthesis, iterative diagnosis, triangulated verification, uncertainty labelling, and accountable disclosure, reframing authorship as auditable process rather than polished output. Integrating mediated action, activity-system contradictions, pragmatics, genre theory, and epistemic cognition, the chapter translates construct logic into scalable pedagogies, evidence-centred assessment architectures, and integrity-by-design governance. It foregrounds equity as a capability condition, embedding culturally responsive prompting, multilingual burden reduction, accessibility-by-design, and privacy-security postures within institutional quality assurance. The result is a tool-agnostic blueprint for future-ready universities that stabilizes validity, trust, and learning under platform volatility.</jats:p>

title: Prompting for Academic Writing and Research
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
a33a6033f3bf398f73b26ab21bb6cfa211ed34c1.abstract: <jats:p>The chapter examines the role of prompt literacy as a structured academic competence in AI-supported writing and research within higher education. It develops and empirically tests a conceptual framework linking prompt quality to academic writing and research performance through the mediating role of cognitive engagement and the moderating influence of institutional academic integrity orientation. Drawing on cognitive, academic literacy, metacognitive, and socio-technical perspectives, the chapter demonstrates that effective prompting is not merely technical but central to scholarly practice. Findings indicate that high-quality prompts enhance analytical depth, coherence, and methodological clarity, particularly when users actively engage with AI outputs. Furthermore, institutional integrity environments strengthen responsible AI use and amplify performance outcomes. The chapter contributes theoretical, pedagogical, and policy insights by positioning prompt literacy as essential for sustaining academic rigor in AI-mediated scholarship.</jats:p>

title: Experiment-specific memory and relaxation structure in graphene transport: a kernel-first state-trajectory analysis
container-title: Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter
7c1703c29eb0feff11158cec1c151106c260aa26.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Graphene transport experiments probe relaxation through different observables, timescales and measurement domains, making direct comparison of reported relaxation parameters difficult. Here we develop a kernel-first, provenance-constrained methodology for determining what aspects of relaxation structure can be identified from heterogeneous transport measurements before assigning them a common physical interpretation. The approach distinguishes measured, processed, fitted and theoretically derived quantities, and separates response magnitude, kernel sensitivity and experimentally observed state evolution. The method is applied to three complementary graphene experiments. Frequency-resolved complex conductivity provides identifiable spectral relaxation descriptors and, where an admissible parametrisation is supported, permits explicit kernel-sensitivity and state-trajectory analysis. Ultrafast electronic heat spreading constrains an additional short-time response relative to an independently determined momentum-relaxation interval, but does not identify a unique kernel time. DC electrical and thermal measurements constrain integrated response weights, geometry dependence and a relative relaxation hierarchy without uniquely determining temporal kernel shape. The three experiments therefore occupy different levels of dynamical identifiability rather than providing interchangeable relaxation times. A localized change in an effective-kernel trajectory is not by itself interpreted as a triggered process. The stronger test requires such a change to reproducibly predict an independently measured dynamical response. We propose a same–device, cross-domain experiment implementing this criterion across controlled state trajectories. The principal contribution is a general analysis methodology for determining what relaxation information heterogeneous measurements support and what additional evidence is required before state-dependent response is promoted to a physical mechanism.</jats:p>

title: Excavating History, Mobilizing Memory
container-title: Moving Memories
83cde5932e9b6a0af93491eec4d035fc0c326670.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter examines two ambulatory, site-specific performances that transformed memorial spaces into sites of remembrance, intercultural dialogue, and historical excavation. These pieces mobilized memories through embodied enactments deeply rooted in the politics of place. The chapter first analyzes Tamar Rogoff’s nostalgic and haunting The Ivye Project (1994), which was performed by a transnational cast of actors, dancers, musicians, and community members in Ivye, Belarus. The immersive piece led audiences through a forest surrounding a mass gravesite, reanimating the town’s Jewish past and commemorating a history suppressed through years of Sovietization. It then discusses Spring in Warsaw by the Israeli collective Public Movement, which reimagined Holocaust tourism and civic ritual through a participatory walk through the Warsaw Ghetto. The chapter argues that site-specific Holocaust performance conjures bodies of the past through the activation of bodies in the present, involving performers and spectators in collective acts of excavation and mourning, accountability and healing.</jats:p>

title: Entangled Histories
container-title: Moving Memories
830a0b79b464393ddf530372769d7faf676dac82.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter discusses two dances by prominent, Black choreographers—Robert Battle and Donald Byrd—set to the music of Erwin Schulhoff, an avant-garde, Jewish composer who perished in a Bavarian labor camp. It considers the composer’s fusion of Black and European aesthetics in relation to modern-dance history and Black-Jewish power dynamics. The chapter analyzes Battle’s No Longer Silent and Donald Byrd’s The Theater of Needless Talents as enactments of multidirectional memory—a concept articulated by Michael Rothberg that rejects competitive approaches to transgenerational trauma by reflecting on the Holocaust in tandem with anti-Black racism and global legacies of colonialism. Battle and Byrd, both of whom identified with Schulhoff’s artistry and marginalization, responded to the Holocaust multidirectionally by using choreographic layering and movement motifs to speak to issues of degradation, persecution, and resistance. The chapter shows how these dances commemorate the Holocaust while encouraging diverse audiences to contemplate ongoing violence toward Black bodies in the United States, as well as other genocides worldwide.</jats:p>

title: Boundary memory in ultrafast field emission: a two-time quantum statistical theory
container-title: Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter
368097744d015db6eba80fbc322d096bfc8ac859.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ultrafast field emission is usually modelled by evaluating the stationary tunnelling current at the instantaneous driving field. We show that this fails whenever the emitting surface has electronic structure near the Fermi level: the vacuum escape channel reacts back on the occupied boundary spectrum that feeds it, and because that spectrum relaxes on a finite timescale the emitted current carries memory of the field’s recent history. Formulating the driven emission problem on the Keldysh contour and propagating the boundary Green functions with a material specific surface spectrum, we find two distinct kinds of memory: a traversal memory that filters and delays the carrier when the driving frequency approaches the tunnelling rate, and a spectral relaxation memory that suppresses and reshapes the current when a pulse drives a thin barrier emitter through the stationary overcoupling turnover. The second can dominate even when the barrier traversal is quasistatic, and predicts a current that falls while the instantaneous transparency still rises. Which memory governs a surface is set by its barrier thickness and its coupling to the vacuum, so the ultrafast waveform distinguishes emitters that the instantaneous theory treats alike.</jats:p>

title: Assistive Monitoring and Support Quality in Cognitive Disability Care
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
db5a35fb0006e94c20dd6e10396daf586441ad4d.abstract: <jats:p>Disability support organisations must maintain safety while supporting independence for people with cognitive disabilities. Traditional supervision relies on routine observation, manual documentation, and reactive intervention, which often creates workload pressure and inconsistent outcomes. Intelligent monitoring systems provide continuous behavioural observation and automated alerts. Many organisations fail to achieve measurable improvement because monitoring data is not integrated into staff workflows, response responsibility, and performance evaluation. This chapter examines monitoring as an organisational decision integration challenge using implementation science, socio-technical theory, and technology adoption theory, explains how monitoring signals influence staff decisions, workflow coordination, and service performance. Introduces the Institutional Integration Framework, which translates monitoring signals into structured workforce response and measurable performance outcomes</jats:p>

title: Comparison of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot Performance in Answering Questions About the Structure of Atoms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
f648170227a2dcf14c457db8406cc2d4610f0113.abstract: <jats:p>In fields with a high concentration of abstract concepts, such as science education, large language models (LLMs) are attracting attention for their potential to provide explanatory and personalized content. This study aims to compare the performance of LLMs ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot in explaining the topic of “The Structure of the Atom” in the context of science education, based on criteria such as scientific accuracy, clarity, pedagogical appropriateness, and misconception risk. Ten questions appropriate for the middle school level were prepared with expert opinion to evaluate the models' response generation capacity and analyzed using rubric-based scoring. The study utilized descriptive statistics, the Friedman test, and the technique for order preference by similarity to ideal solution to determine the models' overall performance levels. The findings indicate that ChatGPT demonstrated consistent and superior performance. The findings guide in terms of science concept teaching, misconception prevention strategies, and scientific accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Quantifying multitime memory in sequential measurement statistics through violations of the quantum regression theorem
container-title: Physical Review A
bd52eccaf16122ebc58103451c3400c4cd32c0d9.abstract: <jats:p>We investigate the presence of memory in the sequential measurement statistics of an open quantum system, as witnessed by the departure from the quantum regression theorem (QRT), that is, the possibility to predict multitime probabilities from one-time reduced dynamical maps. For factorized initial states, we identify an exact decomposition of the two-time propagator into a QRT-like contribution, fully determined by the reduced dynamical map, and a memory term encoding system-environment correlations across the intervention. In the weak-coupling regime, the memory term yields an explicit second-order correction expressed in terms of the reduced map and bath correlation functions. Furthermore, we introduce an operational quantifier of QRT violations based on the distance between exact and QRT-predicted joint probabilities. Benchmarking the framework on a spin-boson model and using a pseudomode embedding as nonperturbative reference, we comprehensively analyze the impact of spectral-density parameters, environmental temperature, and measurement protocols on the non-Markovianity of the multitime statistics. Comparison with a one-time witness shows that reduced-state non-Markovianity and multitime memory are related but inequivalent: the latter, as probed through sequential statistics, is intrinsically protocol dependent and can become visible at higher temporal orders even when lower-order statistics remain compatible with QRT predictions.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive correlates of diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space index in amnestic mild cognitive impairment: a preliminary study
container-title: Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology
1e1bf996cda945b0527e40176b2aa62fdc1d4c7d.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index is an imaging-derived metric related to perivascular water diffusion and has been reported to correlate with global cognitive performance in dementia. However, its associations with specific cognitive functions in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) remain underexplored. This study aimed to characterize the cognitive correlates of the DTI-ALPS index in individuals with amnestic MCI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-sectional study, 57 participants with amnestic MCI underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging and a neuropsychological assessment battery. Correlations between the DTI-ALPS index and performance across the assessed cognitive measures were examined before and after adjustment for age, sex, education, and Fazekas score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior to adjustment, the DTI-ALPS index showed significant positive correlations with global cognitive measures, episodic memory retrieval, and semantic verbal fluency. After controlling for potential confounders, only the correlations with episodic memory and semantic verbal fluency remained significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The DTI-ALPS index remained significantly associated with episodic memory retrieval and semantic verbal fluency in amnestic MCI after adjustment, suggesting a possible link with frontotemporal network-related cognitive functions. Further studies incorporating multimodal imaging and disease-specific biomarkers are warranted to clarify the biological significance of the DTI-ALPS index and its potential clinical relevance in early cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Order-tunable chaotic dynamics, memory-state-dependent coexistence, and reservoir computing in a fractional memfractor-based oscillator
container-title: Physica Scripta
30db02e5d4f782c8c14eeaabc050144f35a705ce.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    In this paper, an autonomous oscillator utilizing a memfractor with fractional-order elements is presented and analyzed with regard to its order-dependent chaotic behavior, memory state-dependent coexistence, and reservoir computing properties. The design includes a Lorenz-like nonlinear element and a memfractor branch where the effective input is generated using the memory state along with a fractional-order accumulation state. The memfractor is first analyzed on an elemental basis through frequency-dependent pinched
                    <jats:italic>v–i</jats:italic>
                    hysteresis loops, which confirm the expected fading-memory signature. Thereafter, the generated oscillator is analyzed using equilibria, stability metrics, phase planes, bifurcations, finite-time Lyapunov analysis, and initial-condition scans. For the default parameter set, nine equilibrium points are detected, including two locally stable equilibria and seven unstable equilibria. Under the same parameters, the system exhibits coexistence between stable equilibrium convergence and bounded chaotic oscillations, mainly selected by the initial memfractor memory state. The memfractor coupling strength controls the transition toward chaos, while the fractional orders tune the intensity of memory-induced divergence. The numerical credibility of the reported regimes is supported by Grünwald–Letnikov and predict–evaluate–correct–evaluate / Adams–Bashforth–Moulton solver cross-validation, together with time-step, simulation-length, and memory-length sensitivity tests. Finally, the oscillator is evaluated as a memory-tunable reservoir on NARMA10 and NARMA20 tasks. In the reservoir-computing tests, the full fractional memfractor configuration gives the lowest representative NARMA10 and NARMA20 prediction errors. The ablation results further indicate that fractional dynamics and memfractor feedback contribute differently to temporal retention and nonlinear prediction. These results show that the fractional memfractor provides a compact mechanism for memory-controlled chaos, coexistence, and reservoir-performance tuning.
                  </jats:p>

title: Cognitive-affective functions, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1
container-title: Journal of Pediatric Psychology
2cb14b067c0eae9b7de70db16716ce2cc29c074b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated associations between social functioning and cognitive-affective functions (CAF), including executive function, face processing, and theory of mind, and neighborhood opportunity, in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Youth with NF1 (n = 37), ages 8–14 (M = 11.8 years), with no prior autism diagnosis, completed assessments of CAF and peer relationships. Parents completed questionnaires on executive function skills, social impairments, and peer relationships. The Childhood Opportunity Index national composite score quantified neighborhood opportunity. Correlation and hierarchical linear regression analyses evaluated associations between social functioning, CAF, and neighborhood opportunity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Executive functioning and neighborhood opportunity were significantly associated with parent reports of social impairments and peer relationships. Executive functioning and facial expression recognition were correlated with self-reported peer relationships, but were not significant in regression models. Facial identity recognition was significantly correlated with social impairments and parent-rated peer relationships. Theory of mind was not associated with any outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings underscore the interplay between CAF, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in children with NF1. Case conceptualizations should integrate social determinants of health with measures of cognition and behavior. Longitudinal research is needed to understand mechanisms driving variability in social outcomes and inform equitable care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Parental scaffolding and cognitive development in early childhood: Insights from a dynamic systems perspective
container-title: Child Development
958b98b1626b048c7804b6008b090f93e5b57b23.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Grounded in dynamic systems theory, which conceptualizes parent–child interactions as evolving systems of reciprocal influence over time, the main objective of this study was to examine which patterns of parent–child scaffolding in a problem-solving situation were associated with children's early cognitive development and to explore whether these patterns were influenced by prior child characteristics. A total of 193 mother–child dyads (109 girls) were observed during a number–image association task at 48 months. Children were predominantly White (95%) and of Canadian or European ethnic background. Three scaffolding phases were examined using the State Space Grid (SSG): modeling (problem-solving strategies are demonstrated by parents), guidance (characterized by shared participation in task execution), and fading (support is gradually withdrawn and greater initiative is shown by children). Only the fading phase was found to be associated with higher complex executive functioning (β = 0.30) and number knowledge (β = 0.42) 1 year later, at 60 months, controlling for prior child cognitive abilities. Furthermore, higher socioeconomic status, receptive vocabulary, and cognitive flexibility at 42 months were positively associated with fading. These findings highlight the importance of interactional processes that promote children's active participation in problem- solving for subsequent cognitive development.</jats:p>
