title: Bridging the Gap: Student Perceptions of Instructor Engagement in Pandemic-Era Online Learning
container-title: The Journal  of Technology, Management, and Applied Engineering
452b4dd3c76ef236fdfaa05cc15c934e6b286cde.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines student perceptions of instructor engagement in online learning environments during the initial onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, with particular attention to differences between students with prior online learning experience and those transitioning from traditional face-to-face instruction. Grounded in Moore’s transactional distance theory, the research explores how sudden shifts in instructional modality influenced students’ perceptions of instructor engagement and identifies strategies that may reduce perceived distance in online learning contexts. Survey data were collected during the summer of 2020 from students enrolled at a regional comprehensive university in the mid-South following the emergency transition to remote instruction. A comparative analysis was conducted across course modalities, focusing on seven survey items related to academic engagement, changes in instructor interaction, and student preferences for engagement. Findings indicate that students with prior experience in online courses perceived less disruption in instructor engagement following the transition, while students who had been enrolled primarily in face-to-face courses reported more noticeable declines. These differences suggest that familiarity with online learning environments may buffer students against perceived losses in engagement during periods of instructional disruption. Overall, this study contributes to the growing body of research on online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic by emphasizing how instructional practices and student experience intersect to influence motivation, engagement, and perceived learning success in online environments.</jats:p>

title: Inclusive Cognitive Design for Global Workforce
container-title: Creative Advantage of Cultural Diversity in Global Business
3c9423f36ac85a9387994c325c3b8405da65dee9.abstract: <jats:p>This paper combines microlearning and inclusivity by suggesting a cognitive design framework that deals with unstable memory at the organizational level. Precarious memory is infrequently addressed in organizational research. This study integrates cognitive science, instructional frameworks, and diversity practices while examining the challenges encountered in VUCA workforce environments. Microlearning as the primary mechanism, facilitated by cultural intelligence and bias awareness, results in task agility and is regulated by psychological safety. The research demonstrates the substantial effectiveness of microlearning in mitigating fragile memory. The results indicate that unstable memory and memory distortion can be trained and alleviated using the proposed framework. This framework makes things more fair and equal and less biased in the workplace. Microlearning's modular approach connects learning with making good decisions, which helps create a workplace that is fair and ethical.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Harmony
container-title: Innovative Strategies for Well-Being and Motivation in Education
010b400f9132cfa7bf09958baa6e7f8172d8af52.abstract: <jats:p>Previous research has shown how motivation and anxiety affect students' academic success, which highlights the importance of implementing strategies in the classroom to promote motivation and manage anxiety in students. Despite these findings, there is a lack of research offering practical guidelines for applying this knowledge in the classrooms. Therefore, the need arises to identify and compile educational strategies and practices that teachers can implement in the classroom to foster motivation and control their students' anxiety. In this chapter, we conducted a literature review aimed at compiling, from an educational scientific evidence approach, various interventions and teaching strategies to promote learning achievement through motivation and anxiety management.</jats:p>

title: Building Bridges
container-title: Innovative Strategies for Well-Being and Motivation in Education
c3f3856b951537f41d996226c542d7ca26a0519b.abstract: <jats:p>In the most recent research on the subject, the student's perception of having the unconditional support of his or her teacher has been shown to be a key variable in the student's school adjustment by promoting his or her school involvement and improving his or her academic performance. However, this knowledge still needs to be refined and the role of each type of support offered by the teacher on the different components of school adjustment still needs to be determined. Two questionnaires, one to assess perceived social support and the other for school involvement, were applied to a sample of 323 secondary school students. The results, extracted by means of a structural regression model, confirm the influence of the perception of the types of teacher support on school adjustment. The data are discussed in terms of previous research and their relevance for the improvement of the teacher-student relationship</jats:p>

title: Engagement and Satisfaction
container-title: Innovative Strategies for Well-Being and Motivation in Education
9de441fffe07454380a91a0e86cf35fa6a66ed49.abstract: <jats:p>Teachers are the pillars of the education system and are responsible for training and educating future citizens. However, nowadays, their level of commitment and satisfaction has sometimes been called into question, as this can directly influence their students. This influence is not only on students' motivation and emotional and personal development but also on students' academic performance. Therefore, the aim of this paper is to explore teachers' perceptions of how their commitment to the teaching profession contributes to students' academic performance and students' views of the impact of their commitment and satisfaction with the teaching profession on their academic performance. To achieve this objective, a non-systematic theoretical review of scientific articles was carried out. This allowed an in-depth unrestricted review of articles published between 2019 and 2024 in databases such as Web of Science and Scopus to study success stories of the influence of Engagement and Satisfaction from the point of view of both teachers and students.</jats:p>

title: Digital Quality Assurance for Refugee Higher Education
container-title: Harnessing Digital Platforms for Quality Assurance and Monitoring in Higher Education
be7e6eff4a1727c47e4a282be62ea19a563a46f3.abstract: <jats:p>The digital turn in higher education has redefined how quality is conceptualised, delivered, and measured, yet refugee learners continue to be excluded from these transformative shifts. Among them, the Rohingya refugees in India remain structurally marginalised, with little access to accredited or quality-assured higher-education opportunities. This chapter investigates how digital quality assurance frameworks can close these educational divides by drawing comparative lessons from Germany's refugee integration model. Through a doctrinal and expert-opinion legal-policy approach, the study interprets the role of technology, regulation, and institutional accountability in building inclusive quality systems. It analyses Germany's Akkreditierungsrat standards, DAAD Integra initiatives, and data-driven monitoring as benchmarks for digital assurance, then contrasts them with India's digital ecosystem within the framework of the National Education Policy 2020. The research develops a Digital Quality Assurance for Refugee Education model that aligns with SDG 4 and SDG 16.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Adaptation and Leadership in AI-Augmented Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Responsible AI Governance in Higher Education Management for Creative Public Sector Innovation
a5612c037c0c5391ee895bba1a4fc5ae65f530b1.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI poses pressing governance challenges regarding the future of human-AI interaction and how it enhances or diminishes the cognitive capabilities, professional role, and leadership of academic professionals. Three cognitive adaptation patterns emerge from the analysis of the qualitative data (retrieved from the interviews) and the quantitative data (PLS-SEM survey): AI Augmentation, AI Dependency, and AI Co-construction. The positive relationship between adaptation outcomes and AI trust is supported by PLS-SEM, with the cognitive load change as a mediator and the organisational learning orientation as a moderator, the most significant institutional factor influencing adaptation outcomes. The chapter suggests embedding metacognition and AI literacy in workforce governance, institutional reflection in HR and L&D processes, and complementarity guardrails. For practical governance tools for adopting responsible AI in higher education, a validated diagnostic instrument and a Human-AI Capability Convergence Model are provided.</jats:p>

title: An Individualized Approach to Augmentative and Alternative Communication for Cortical Visual Impairment: One Family's Progression Toward an Accessible Language System
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
f0ff7edf9656cc552dd1d0ce7c53989cc10572bd.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Speech-language pathologists report a desire for guidance to develop and maintain augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) supports that are customized and visually accessible for individuals with cortical visual impairment (CVI; Boster et al., 2021). In 2023, Wilkinson et al. introduced the “CVI/AAC Framework” that offered initial evidence-based considerations and data collection prompts to address this clinical challenge. The current article was written to illustrate the process of the clinical application of the CVI/AAC Framework for a young child with cerebral palsy and concomitant CVI. By demonstrating the team efforts to build a developmentally appropriate aided AAC system that was responsive to the child's CVI and motor support needs, we hope to demonstrate the utility of the framework and promote clinical uptake for decision making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The team, which included clinicians, other professionals, and the child's mother, implemented an iterative approach to AAC assessment and implementation based on ongoing discussions surrounding the CVI/AAC Framework domains and the child's progress. The relative frequency of different topics of discussion and the subsequent types of decisions made were quantified to illustrate the clinical process. Furthermore, a detailed case analysis of the contents of the discussion were extracted from the transcripts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The team met collaboratively for 8 months, resulting in 13 meetings. A total of 97 topics were discussed and coded related to the CVI/AAC Framework or general AAC assessment. Of the topics related to the framework, Domain 1 (characteristics of the individual) accounted for the most discussions followed by Domain 3 (AAC system design choices). Meeting documentation and screen captures of the child's AAC system across time demonstrated changes in the child's linguistic and visual functioning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This clinical focus article illustrates a starting point for implementation of the CVI/AAC Framework as a complementary approach to typical AAC assessment procedures. This approach should prompt clinicians to make individualized AAC changes that support meaningful communication and participation and provide a basis for future systematic research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Supplemental Material:</jats:title>

                    </jats:p>

title: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy–Based Digital Interventions for Illicit Substance Use Disorders: Scoping Review of Intervention Design, Efficacy Indicators, and Methodological Gaps
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
9d1858cff34c91ccfc45c7d996e799804ca90d99.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Illicit substance use disorders (SUDs) are escalating globally; yet, social stigma and legal barriers restrict access to conventional treatment, and existing research remains skewed toward alcohol and nicotine. Digital interventions incorporating cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) offer a discreet, scalable alternative.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This scoping review maps how CBT-based digital interventions for illicit SUDs are designed and delivered across platforms, identifying their theoretical frameworks, functional components, outcome indicators, and reported methodological limitations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) scoping review methodology and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews). Six databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, APA PsycINFO, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane Library, and CINAHL) were searched from inception to June 28, 2026, without language, date, or study design limits, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching (July 3, 2026). Eligible studies were empirical primary studies quantitatively evaluating digital interventions incorporating CBT for illicit or nonprescribed substance use; alcohol- or nicotine-only populations were excluded. Three reviewers independently screened and charted all studies, with disagreements resolved by consensus or adjudication. Data were synthesized narratively, with tables, figures, and an evidence gap map.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifty-six studies published between 2008 and 2026, drawn from 47 distinct participant samples, met the eligibility criteria. Most were conducted in North America (40/56, 71.4%) and used randomized controlled designs (39/56, 69.6%). Polysubstance-using populations were most frequently targeted (32/56, 57.1%), followed by cannabis (13/56, 23.2%), opioids (6/56, 10.7%), and stimulants (5/56, 8.9%). Interventions were delivered mainly via web (24/56, 42.9%) or app (24/56, 42.9%) platforms, and most (49/56, 87.5%) were grounded in traditional CBT, most often combined with contingency management (18/56, 32.1%) or motivational interviewing (17/56, 30.4%). Core functional components included therapeutic intervention (55/56, 98.2%), self-tracking and notification (25/56, 44.6%), reward (24/56, 42.9%), and support and feedback (21/56, 37.5%). Primary outcomes focused on substance use and abstinence (41/56, 73.2%), retention/feasibility (16/56, 28.6%), and mental health status or coping skills (14/56, 25%). Author-reported limitations were predominantly participant-level (52/56, 92.9%), measurement-level (43/56, 76.8%), study-level (34/56, 60.7%), and intervention-level (25/56, 44.6%) domains.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Unlike previous reviews confined to a single substance or delivery platform, this review is innovative in mapping CBT-based digital interventions across the full spectrum of illicit substances, including polysubstance use, and in linking their functional components to intended therapeutic mechanisms. It thereby contributes to the development of these technologies and, by synthesizing author-reported limitations, proposes methodological improvements for their future evaluation. At present, CBT-based digital interventions are best positioned as adjuncts that extend the reach and continuity of existing addiction care rather than as stand-alone substitutes for it; substance-specific customization, objective outcome measures, and modular trial designs are needed to establish them as scalable clinical tools.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Multi-model ensemble projections of African humid heat extremes and their implications for future health studies
container-title: Environmental Research: Health
71c28d244b3645341138d8ea6a4574cf40f14c6b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Global warming and extreme heat events have well-documented adverse effects on human health. As a first step to understand the possible future risk for heat-related illness and mortality, this study analyzes climate model projections to constrain model variability and spread related to humid heat extremes over Africa. Using CMIP6, CESM2-LE, CORDEX and CMIP5 models, we examine the impacts of model uncertainty, horizontal resolution, and internal variability on projections of heat indices, including wet bulb temperature, wet bulb globe temperature, Humidex, and the extended heat index, over the next century. Across resolutions and model types, humid heat projections under moderate greenhouse gas (GHG) emission scenarios (SSP245/RCP45) indicate that Sub-Saharan Africa will experience a higher count of extreme heat events over the next century compared to the rest of the continent. Within CESM2-LE, the trends in humid heat metrics are driven almost entirely by external forcings (i.e. increasing GHG emissions), except in parts of Central, Northeast, and Southeast Africa, where natural variability accounts for roughly 10%–18% of the total variance. Model resolution has a significant impact on the simulated number of extreme humid heat events; low-resolution models from CMIP5 project roughly 40–80 more extreme event days per year over Central Africa by the end of the century compared to their corresponding downscaled CORDEX models. This work serves as a key precursor to future studies projecting heat-health outcomes due to climate change over Africa.</jats:p>

title: AttenResUNet: An RFI Detection Model Based on the AttenRes Architecture
container-title: Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics
0a352f0ee784005a79843fe4da749fce11f5fdcc.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate classification and detection of Radio Frequency Interference (RFI) is a core step in the preprocessing of radio astronomy observational data, which directly affects the quality of astronomical signal extraction and analysis. Traditional threshold-based detection methods rely on manual parameter tuning, making it difficult to set appropriate thresholds and handle increasingly complex and diverse types of RFI. Since 2017, UNet-based models have become a popular research approach for RFI mitigation. However, conventional UNet-like models suffer from drawbacks such as high computational cost, easy loss of detailed information during deep feature propagation, and insufficient detection accuracy for small-scale RFI. To cope with these situations, this paper proposes the AttenResUNet model, which integrates strip pooling enhancement, adaptive attention weight calculation, and a blocking mechanism to construct an efficient and accurate multi-class RFI detection framework. Experimental results on the RFI image data set show that the average F1-score of the proposed model after excluding the background category is improved by more than 20% compared with threshold-based methods. For weak narrowband RFI, the F1-score is increased by 5% relative to traditional UNet, ResUNet, and other models, while the training cost is reduced by over 60%. The model enables fine-grained classification and detection of five RFI categories under limited computing resources, providing a new technical route for efficient processing of radio astronomy data. Validation experiments demonstrate that data denoised by our model yields significantly improved signal-to-noise ratio in pulsar search images for NGC 6517 B, F and G, with sharper peaks and more distinct pulsar characteristics.</jats:p>

title: Mental Health Policy Personnel and Collaborators

aa86cad111b5f9914e7e1de3b59e0f447691d4c2.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The purpose of the current chapter is to guide school social workers in their understanding of the mental health policy landscape and how policy impacts their profession and opportunities for collaboration with individuals in their school, district, and community. The chapter reviews the current state of student mental health and the role of school social workers, provides a case study, and delves into best practices to guide school social workers in ways they can advocate for mental health policy at the district, state, and federal level. This chapter also provides concrete guidance outlining how social workers can find relevant policies impacting their role and their local school district, including how to secure mental health funding. Additionally, the chapter provides steps to engage in data collection to ultimately understand mental health needs and steps to advocate for student mental health services, including the development of school–community partnerships to support these services.</jats:p>

title: Grant Funders
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
c29098cdc57527f83e18e4adec60012809680d7a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Grant funding can help expand school social work services in a school district as a means of meeting the social-emotional learning and mental health needs of all students. This chapter explores grant-funding opportunities, the importance of collaboration when seeking funding, understanding grant requirements, and how seeking grant funding supports the tenets of the national school social work model. It also explores the challenges and issues of grant funding. While school social workers can leverage grants to address systemic inequities within the home–school–community, the process by which grants are allocated can also create inequities at the same time. Best practices that could increase the likelihood of obtaining grant funding are provided.</jats:p>

title: Certification and Licensure Boards
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
da35059ce0b69148a872f65e2e5b4a332d64ef62.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Certification and Licensure Board chapter examines the role of school social workers, the challenges in unifying certification and licensure requirements across states, and the importance of working with key personnel to promote a national approach to school social work certification. The challenges discussed in this review highlight barriers such as a lack of consistent requirements across states to practice as a school social worker, burdens experienced by historically marginalized candidates, and issues ensuring title protection. The chapter concludes with recommended best practices to support utilizing the SSWAA National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0 in collaborating with school social work state professional associations, school social work preparation programs, policymakers, and state regulatory boards to advocate for title protection and the continuity of certification and licensure of highly qualified school social workers across states.</jats:p>

title: Engaging with the State Education Agency
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
5c7b5884ab06f4174c4ca2fa2ca1477504dadc4f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The purpose of this chapter is to explain the role of the state education agency (SEA), provide rationale for the importance of engagement with the SEA, the presence of school social work in the SEA, and the connection between engaging with the SEA and the SSWAA National Practice Model 2.0. Information was gathered from SEA websites, published articles, experience, and knowledge from SEA employees. The results of this inquiry show various forms of SEAs with similar, yet varying roles. Regardless of these variations, school social workers have many practical options for how and why to engage with the state SEA.</jats:p>

title: District and School-Building Administrators
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
d8f675a5114601b14f2d721c58175885535e3b72.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter discusses how school social workers can build partnerships with school boards, district administrators, and building-level administrators. A key aspect of this is advocating for how their professional skills align with and advance their mission, vision, and values. Defining and clarifying roles, responsibilities, and expectations for all parties can develop strong communication and relationships with administration on all levels. Implementing the SSWAA National Practice Model 2.0 five domains provides a framework for school social workers to understand the values, domains, focus areas, and professional activities of school social workers (Tan & SSWWA, 2024). Building partnerships and the importance of data collection are discussed as recommended best practices for school social workers.</jats:p>

title: District Board of Education
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
8b8d9bc886aa6adaed2a58f7739ad967d484a19f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter on working with the District Board of Education explores the ethical and practical considerations for school social workers engaging with elected officials and advocating for policy changes. School social workers have an ethical obligation to promote social justice and advocate for policies that benefit all students, particularly those who are historically excluded or marginalized. In alignment with the School Social Work National Practice Model, the authors emphasize the importance of using interpersonal skills, research skills, and policy knowledge to effectively influence policy decisions. The chapter concludes with a call for school social workers to embrace their role as advocates and to work toward creating more equitable policies for all students.</jats:p>

title: Supervisors of School Social Workers
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
1f03ea65844dcc84e4ec73e76c728a6072556ad6.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter explores the primary components of school social work supervision and provides actionable examples of supervision topics to be used with supervisees. Supervision of school social workers is a primary component of ethical practice and a tool for implementing the National School Social Work Model 2.0. It is through supervision by a fellow practitioner that issues and challenges in the school setting can be addressed. The chapter identifies the professional and supervisory challenges that exist in the supervision of school social workers, as well as the knowledge base that leads to student success. Using the updated national model as a guide, supervision can expand the policy, practice, leadership, and advocacy knowledge of those being supervised, as well as support equity, ethics, and standards within the school setting.</jats:p>

title: Allied Professionals
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
8bcc5c21a8c24b8fcaf20e2d7899f391937c6b0c.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter discusses wide-ranging nuances of working with allied professionals in school settings, including common complexities, challenges, and benefits. By highlighting key components of the SSWAA National Practice Model 2.0, the chapter illuminates how school social workers can empower students and schools to strengthen educational well-being by intentionally collaborating in effective ways with their allied colleagues. The chapter emphasizes that intentional communication, role clarity, and collaborative problem-solving are essential for reducing role conflict and empowering schools to better meet the academic, socioemotional, and mental health needs of students and families, particularly with increasingly complex and evolving educational and community contexts.</jats:p>

title: P–12 Educators and Teachers
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
73e5260639044ccc111c7af5d7963e9c700b9545.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter, co-authored by a teacher and a school social work academic, explores the contributions that teachers make to student well-being. It highlights teachers’ unique positioning to address student wellness individually and structurally. It extends from the new National SSW model to provide explicit guidance to school social workers about how they can make the most of teachers’ student support capacities via professional development, inclusion in student support systems and collaboration. The authors also share suggestions for working with teachers who are hesitant to engage with school social workers or to address wellness concerns that emerge with their own students.</jats:p>

title: Parents and Families
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
a25e2fa80673f988ad727917f02fcfd119d6cab3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This chapter reviews the benefits of home–school–community partnerships in supporting student academics, socio-emotional well-being, mental health, and school climate. School social workers are well-positioned to promote meaningful parent and family engagement in schools. Parent and family engagement has myriad benefits for families, children, and schools. Traditionally, school–family partnerships do not emphasize equity and mutual reciprocity. The chapter identifies contemporary challenges and structural barriers that caregivers face and offers recommendations for school social workers to build equitable relationships with families, including working with families from a strengths-based and trauma-informed perspective. Recommendations draw on the SSWAA National Practice Model 2.0 to highlight professional activities school social workers can utilize to build strong home–school–community relationships and create meaningful and long-lasting engagement with families. Finally, recommendations for best practices are shared.</jats:p>

title: Community Agencies and After-school Programs
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
97b2b5687abc2ded8cfa82354ea40fb70788e74b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Community agencies and after-school programs extend learning, enrichment, and care into critical hours beyond the school day, offering safe, supportive environments especially vital for youth in under-resourced communities. School social workers (SSWers) serve as key connectors, linking students and families with these opportunities and fostering holistic support across home, school, and community. Yet partnerships face persistent barriers, including attendance, transportation, eligibility restrictions, limited family engagement, and staff fatigue—challenges intensified by a socio-political climate that threatens equity-focused and mental health services. This chapter explores these complexities while highlighting strategies for collaboration, advocacy, and leadership through the National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0. It emphasizes how SSWers can help transform after-school and community-based programs into spaces of empowerment, resilience, and systemic change that expand opportunities for all students.</jats:p>

title: University Educators
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
760ece7090ecb546452979d21ba065c59b57f77e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>University educators play a pivotal role in ensuring that school social workers (SSWers) are consistently and effectively prepared to meet the unique demands of their profession by aligning their curricula with the National Model for School Social Work Practice 2.0 (National Model for SSW Practice). Varying state standards for education and certification create inconsistency in SSWer roles and functions. The National Model for SSW Practice provides a framework of essential knowledge and skills. This chapter explores recommendations to integrate the National Model for SSW Practice into higher education by aligning the National Model for SSW Practice with the Council on Social Work Education (CSWE) Competencies, which is important to ensure that social work programs prepare students to meet both accreditation requirements and the specialized demands of school social work. A “crosswalk” was developed that aligns school social work–specific components (knowledge and skills) with the National Model for SSW Practice’s elements and domains, as well as with the nine CSWE competencies. This alignment provides a tool for university educators to track the distribution of National Model for SSW Practice elements throughout their curriculum, including courses, certificates, and practicum placements. This approach also helps in designing assessments and can be shared with practicum supervisors to ensure students receive consistent training that bridges theoretical knowledge with practical application. By using the National Model for SSW Practice to guide curriculum development and collaborating with state departments of education, higher education institutions can prepare SSWers equipped with the knowledge and skills needed for the challenges of working within the school setting.</jats:p>

title: Internship Supervisors
container-title: Implementation Guide: The National School Social Work Practice Model 2.0
4a93cce5e145ab9b86f52c96de3bb6e65075bbae.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>SSW Internship Instructors chapter outlines the key components in creating a student learning program that contributes to an environment for student success. An effective relationship between the internship instructor and student should be the foundation. This allows for the key components of consistent and meaningful supervision, detailed and constructive feedback, a structured learning plan, and exposure to learning opportunities that meet the nine EPAS competencies and teach best practices to be developed. The chapter discusses the important role instructors have in supporting students as they develop a framework and perspective to be successful. A successful internship experience helps to equip the student with skills to encounter the clinical, cultural, and ethical situations they might face in the future as school social workers.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Digital Twins and Blockchain Ecosystems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Next-Generation Supply Chain Management in the Industrial Metaverse
800c4603905b0b481af418f93c27b335627b538c.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter develops an architecture for combining cognitive digital twins with blockchain ecosystems to deliver predictive business intelligence in the industrial metaverse. It argues that digital-twin initiatives create value only when operational telemetry, semantic context, decision models, and human governance are connected through trusted data-sharing and executable coordination mechanisms. Drawing on research in digital twins, industrial metaverse design, blockchain-enabled provenance, smart contracts, human-centric manufacturing, and explainable AI, the chapter proposes a layered reference architecture, performance metrics, implementation logic, and governance controls. It also examines persistent challenges, including semantic fragmentation, model drift, latency, privacy, interoperability, energy cost, and the oracle problem. The chapter concludes with design recommendations and a research agenda for resilient, trustworthy, and economically useful industrial intelligence systems across networked industrial-metaverse platforms and ecosystems.</jats:p>

title: Social Efficiency in Contemporary Social Systems
container-title: Collective Action and Social Regulation in Complex Societies
061e73d8bd6c070c263a414b9d8abf6108537c36.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines social efficiency as a key analytical category for evaluating contemporary social systems and public policies. Given the limitations of traditional economic-only approaches, the research systematizes theoretical perspectives and proposes an interdisciplinary integrative model for assessment. This model links objectives, resources, processes, and long-term impacts within a unified framework. Key findings highlight the necessity of integrated evaluation systems, improved institutional coordination, and innovative digital tools. The results offer practical implications for both academic research and public governance, fostering sustainable and effective social policies.</jats:p>

title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
Beyond Recognition
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
8d55c03606f397dfebd690ec5704784da2344f3c.abstract: <jats:p>Current e-learning systems are still not well-suited to learn in real-time as individuals' emotional and cognitive state. The chapter presents AIALE (Affective Intelligence Adaptive Learning Engine), a multimodal system capable of embedding facial coding, bio signals, keystroke dynamics and eye-tracking in a single pipeline and with sub-500ms inference latency. The AIALE's three-tier architecture consists of a deep learning-based effect inference, a reinforcement learning-based curriculum control and a pedagogic intervention broker. AIALE was tested with 214 university students from four disciplines and led to statistically significant increases in knowledge gain (31% above that of a knowledge-adaptive baseline) as well as to an increase in engagement duration and a balance of cognitive load, compared to a knowledge-adaptive baseline and a non-adaptive control. An ablation analysis shows that the most significant affective dimensions for adaptive interventions' quality are confusion and cognitive load detection. The chapter also introduces five research gaps and explores emerging research avenues such as generative AI tutoring agents and explainable affective adaptation.</jats:p>

title: Camera-Based Deep Learning Framework for Real-Time Emotion-Aware Engagement Detection in E-Learning
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
10cfc4979912c42a01924f13bd2193ca5e197ab1.abstract: <jats:p>The explosive expansion of digital learning platforms has revolutionized the manner in which students access, consume, and interact with academic content. Sustaining high levels of engagement within online spaces, though, remains perhaps the most critical challenge facing higher education. Conventional methods of measuring engagement—e.g., tracking presence, post-session questionnaires, or physiological sensors—are intrusively burdensome, not very reliable, and less than ideal for widespread implementation. Technological developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning provide non-invasive means, notably via camera-based emotion detection systems that are able to track and decipher learner engagement real-time. This chapter suggests a human-focused deep learning approach that incorporates facial emotion detection with adaptive learning routes to boost learner engagement and mental growth in e-learning contexts.</jats:p>

title: Challenges and Ethical Considerations in Gamified and Cognitive Learning in Cybersecurity Education
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
fe7c56a27e63d56369910ade1fabf1dae4d33295.abstract: <jats:p>Gamified and cognitive learning in cybersecurity education is gaining popularity, but it brings its own set of challenges, particularly when it comes to ethics. Training through games can sharpen technical skills, yet there's always the risk of blurring the lines between ethical hacking and actual cybercrime. Some learners may be tempted to misuse their knowledge, especially if ethical considerations aren't woven into the experience from the start. Then there's the question of real-world readiness—does solving puzzles in a simulated environment translate to handling live cyber threats? Beyond that, data privacy is a concern. Gamified platforms track progress, but how much of that data should they collect, and who gets access? And let's not ignore the psychology behind game mechanics, does intense competition fuel motivation or push players toward reckless behavior? The key lies in balance. Industry and academia need to step in with clear ethical guidelines, ensuring that gamification encourages responsibility alongside skill-building. A well-designed system can use storytelling, role-playing, and collaborative challenges to reinforce ethical decision-making rather than just technical mastery. AI could play a role in adapting training to individuals, but it raises ethical dilemmas. Cybersecurity threats are constantly changing, so training must evolve too. Gamified education can be a powerful tool, but only if it's designed with ethics at its core.</jats:p>

title: Deep Learning Architectures for Real-Time Emotion and Engagement Detection in E-Learning Platforms
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
f9731fd32e93095cf320cc72899c5ae1486d338c.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of deep learning into e-learning environments has revolutionised the way learners interact with educational content. This study explores the design and implementation of deep learning architectures for real-time emotion and engagement detection in e-learning platforms. By leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and transformer-based models, the proposed framework captures multimodal data such as facial expressions, speech tone, eye movement, and physiological signals to assess learners' emotional states and engagement levels dynamically. The system provides adaptive feedback to instructors and personalised interventions to learners, enhancing cognitive growth and overall learning outcomes. The research also discusses the challenges of real-time processing, model interpretability, data privacy, and ethical considerations associated with emotion recognition technologies in education.</jats:p>

title: Deep Learning for Modern E-Learning Systems
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
9aaf4dfff445fa1aad16b80d1c5376fcd12ec6c4.abstract: <jats:p>Models that learn from users and content interact at scale. This chapter articulates the many uses of highly layered neural networks in personalization, applied feedback, and text, speech, code, image, and video assistance. The main model families are described: CNNs, RNNs / LSTMs, transformers, autoencoders, and other generative models; as are the approaches to training, optimizing, regularizing, and deploying models. Representation learning from unstructured data, adaptive pathways, engagement and emotion detection, and predicting performance and studying are learning outcomes that guide model choice. System elements include data gathering, analytics, model serving in-cloud or on-device, and scale. Intelligent tutoring, recommendation, auto-grading, and dialogue systems on modern platforms are current use cases. Trade-offs include privacy, sparse supervision, bias, lack of explainability, seamlessness to legacy systems, and computation cost. Real-world deployments, both successful and not, are the focus of the illustrative case studies. The chapter's focus is on core techniques and design choices to build the next generation of e-learning systems.</jats:p>

title: Deep Learning-Driven Emotion Recognition for Personalized and Adaptive E-Learning Systems
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
ce676f08ce46956bb22f53f59a27b6cbe5ec864b.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores how deep learning–based emotion recognition enhances student engagement and cognitive growth in e-learning environments. By leveraging CNN and LSTM architectures, the proposed framework detects learners' emotions from facial and behavioral cues in real time, enabling adaptive instructional responses. Through camera-based, non-invasive monitoring, emotions such as confusion, curiosity, or satisfaction are quantified to personalize learning experiences and improve retention. The chapter also discusses dataset selection, model design, and integration into Learning Management Systems (LMS). Case insights demonstrate how emotion-aware systems foster empathy, motivation, and inclusivity in digital education. Ethical considerations privacy, fairness, and explainability are addressed to ensure responsible AI deployment. The study establishes emotion recognition as a cornerstone for intelligent, adaptive, and human-centered e-learning ecosystems that align technology with emotional intelligence and pedagogical effectiveness.</jats:p>

title: How Gamification Mechanics Improve Cybersecurity Learning Retention
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
e507f4e7f41e686a6ea10856a0a000bbacf36594.abstract: <jats:p>Gamification taps into how the brain processes rewards, emotions, and repetition, making it a powerful tool for cybersecurity education. When learners engage with challenges that trigger dopamine release—like solving puzzles, earning achievements, or progressing through a story—retention improves. The way emotions shape memory also plays a role; high-stakes simulations and immersive storytelling make security concepts stick. Incorporating game mechanics, such as real-time feedback, narrative-driven exercises, and adaptive difficulty, strengthens learning. Capture the Flag competitions and VR-based training reinforce hands-on skills, while spaced repetition counters memory decay. More than just engagement, this approach helps reduce anxiety by creating a safe space for trial and error, building confidence without the fear of real-world consequences. As AI begins to refine personalized learning paths, cybersecurity training can adapt to individual strengths and weaknesses. Long-term, this shift could shape a more prepared, responsive workforce—one that learns through experience, not just theory. But with any gamified system, balance is key.</jats:p>

title: Natural Language Processing for Interactive Learning Experiences
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
987c3de7f795db1cc232a6a4b1b49390a428ce0f.abstract: <jats:p>Natural Language Processing (NLP) has become a core component for next generation e-learning ecosystems, especially in content delivery. It enables platforms to understand, respond and adapt to individual learners. With the rise of deep learning models especially transformer based architectures, NLP now offers state of the art capabilities for real-time interaction, personalized feedback, and adaptive learning pathways. This chapter examines NLP-driven systems powered by deep learning to enhance learner engagement, motivation, and cognitive development. It is developed by converting static educational materials into dynamic, conversational, and highly interactive experiences. The key ideas in this chapter includes understanding text, language models that can generate responses, intelligent tutoring systems, automatic grading, feedback that considers emotions, and learning that uses multiple types of media (such as text, audio, and images). Practical use cases and emerging research trends are highlighted. Ethical, pedagogical and technological challenges are also discussed.</jats:p>

title: Passive Learning to Active Engagement
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
eacaa5f4ae36bc7dc2909810ec0a52e6a7081ebd.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid evolution of digital technologies has transformed the educational landscape, challenging traditional passive learning models and emphasizing the need for active engagement in deep learning. Passive learning, characterized by one-way information delivery and limited learner interaction, often results in superficial comprehension and low retention. In contrast, active engagement leverages interactive digital tools, collaborative strategies, and learner-centered approaches to foster critical thinking, problem-solving, and meaningful knowledge construction. This chapter explores the theoretical underpinnings of passive and active learning, examines the pedagogical shift facilitated by digital technologies, and highlights effective strategies for promoting deep learning in contemporary educational environments. Case studies from diverse educational contexts illustrate how digital pedagogy can bridge the gap between passive reception and active participation, ultimately enhancing learner motivation, engagement, and long-term retention.</jats:p>

title: Real-Time Multimodal Engagement Detection in E-Learning
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
cc8c8875c98107da22dfb5309173f1535042c386.abstract: <jats:p>The transition from in-person classrooms to digital and hybrid modes of learning has created new opportunities but has also posed several serious problems for education. One of the most key problems is the measurement of student engagement. This chapter discusses the use of deep learning for multimodal engagement detection to analyze visual data, auditory data, and behavioral data. By combining these signals, the adaptive feedback loops can be built supporting the learning. This chapter presents artificial intelligence together with psychological theories of the motivation, attention, and cognitive load in order to design human-centered environments that help teachers to be more efficient. Ethical issues like privacy, consent, and bias are dealt with to make sure they are utilized in a responsible manner. The chapter includes case studies from India and also other parts of the globe, showing the opportunities and challenges. The design of the system is proposed as a framework including pipelines, and integration with learning platforms.</jats:p>

title: The Psychology of Deep Learning for Student Engagement and Cognitive Development
container-title: Deep Learning for Engagement and Cognitive Growth in E-Learning
388c0f1038cc6f8828ff44b71c150147ada103bd.abstract: <jats:p>Against the background of deep learning for engagement and cognitive growth in e-learning, the purpose of this chapter is to discuss findings from a real-world case study implementation at a Higher Education Institution (HEI) in Namibia. Towards addressing the psychology of deep learning for student engagement and cognitive development by reconfiguring e-learning accessibility via mobile technologies, the main focus of the chapter will be on tools, platforms, and gaps, as well as challenges and limitations, related to e-learning ecosystems. Future research directions based on the findings will be presented in order to come to conclusions toward smarter, fairer, human-centered learning.</jats:p>

title: A3 Model in Indian Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
c1ad93ee7e0991c260ac643de8c3fa1e55541ddd.abstract: <jats:p>The appearance of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Indian academic spaces has ushered in a wave of revolutionary changes, bringing new tools like intelligent automation, supporting governance, intelligent data-based decisions, and the like. This subchapter attempts to bring out a framework, A3 Model, where Agentic AI, Administrative Resilience, and Educational Excellence are offered within one overarching design from a more applied framework. The chapter goes on with an empirical inquiry where mixed methods and PLS-SEM are used on data from Indian universities, focusing on how Agentic AI shapes institutional responsiveness and academic performance. The results show that there exists a strong and positive connection among the capabilities of AI, the existence of an agile organization, and the realization of desirable academic outcomes, but most significantly, the interaction of those effects in the context of escalating and fostering the productive and efficient administration within the higher education system.</jats:p>

title: Collaborative Knowledge Distillation and Reinforcement Learning for Automated Ticket Triage in Large-Scale Production Systems
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
8b0253b0417c564346ca68d9c57a0a0b2b97123a.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In large-scale enterprise environments, growing system complexity makes failures inevitable, threatening business continuity and customer satisfaction. To maintain system stability, efficient ticket triage is crucial for timely incident resolution. However, it remains a knowledge-intensive task requiring substantial domain expertise and detailed analysis, revealing the limitations of traditional rule-based and text-based methods. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new possibilities for automating triage through their remarkable reasoning and language capabilities. Yet, in industrial settings, LLMs often struggle to leverage domain-knowledge essential for accurate triage. We present
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">CoTriage</jats:italic>
                    , a practical and scalable end-to-end automated ticket triage system, designed and deployed for real-world industrial scenarios.
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">CoTriage</jats:italic>
                    leverages novel collaboration between large and small models: a small set of labeled tickets is used to distill high-quality LLM reasoning into a lightweight model, which is further optimized through a self-reinforcement mechanism. The refined triager then acts as a reward model to fine-tune a ticket summarizer using reinforcement learning. Comprehensive experiments conducted in the production environment of ByteDance, a leading global online video service provider, demonstrate the effectiveness of CoTriage, reducing the average triage time to 15.0 seconds and significantly enhancing operational efficiency and accelerating incident resolution in practice.
                  </jats:p>

title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
ESL Classrooms in the Age of AI
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
9ec5be19b6f57cc824ddd32998fbae5b92f230e2.abstract: <jats:p>Between 2020 and 2025, EFL and ESL classrooms have undergone rapid platformization, with AI writing tutors, learning management systems, and online proctoring becoming central to instruction and assessment. This chapter examines how these AI-mediated technologies reshape gender dynamics in language education, with attention to learners outside the traditional gender binary. Combining a critical narrative review (2020-2025) with a structured walkthrough of ten platforms evaluated against a three-criterion Gender-Inclusivity Audit, the chapter finds uneven patterns: while flagship generative AI has improved its handling of gender-neutral pronouns, legacy writing-evaluation tools, learning management systems, and biometric proctoring continue to enforce binary, Western-normative baselines. The chapter contributes a comparative theoretical synthesis, empirical evidence on algorithmic bias, and a five-step practitioner framework, arguing that educational equity requires gender-responsive, decolonially-grounded design rather than superficial gender-neutrality.</jats:p>

title: Gender Differences in English Language Acquisition
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
8696b21f04f37644305f240d49870b22729864c7.abstract: <jats:p>Learning English language is a process that is influenced by gender differences that impact the motivation and attitudes that the learners have towards it and patterns of interaction in the classroom. Research has shown that the preferences and methods of learning, and affective reactions of both males and females' learners might differ and be determined in advance by the sociocultural challenges, mode of thinking or earlier experiences with language. Motivation- Intrinsic and extrinsic-The differences in motivation (in persistence, effort, and goal orientation) across gender in language learning. The disposition to the English language is also diversified in the shape of the visions of its utilization, social competence, and personal pertinence that dictate the readiness of the learner to the process of language acquisition and to run the risks. The other field that there will be differences in gender in terms of classroom interaction is that the female gender will be more active when it comes to collaboration and oral communication.</jats:p>

title: Gendered Dimensions of Emotional Labor in Technology-Mediated English Language Learning
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
afa9c09180f8ae02239c558e1d2aff4bf8c0c337.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education is widely framed in terms of efficiency and personalization. This chapter argues that such framings obscure a more consequential transformation: the redistribution of emotional labor across teachers, learners, and algorithmic systems along gendered lines. Drawing on Hochschild's emotional labor theory, Butler's gender performativity framework, and self-determination theory, it examines how AI systems simulate empathy, encode gendered service scripts, and restructure the affective architecture of language learning without eliminating the human burden of care. To conceptualize this restructuring, the chapter proposes the Gender-Responsive Affective Redistribution framework, which treats AI integration as affective restructuring rather than technological enhancement, and introduces the concept of autonomy drift to describe the gradual displacement of self-regulated learning by system-initiated prompts.</jats:p>

title: Inclusive English Language Instruction Through Flipped Learning
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
94fc234e27e459b844bcbf8fb29984ce7d27d185.abstract: <jats:p>The influence of socio-cultural variables on the development of the English language is not a new phenomenon, and gender is among the most significant yet complex aspects. Gender is not the only factor that determines learners' linguistic identity. Still, it is also a mediating factor in terms of access, participation, confidence, and achievement in an English language learning environment. Therefore, Flipped Learning (FL) has emerged as a revolutionary learning philosophy that is restoring the aspect of teachers and learners where direct instruction is outside the classroom and classroom time is spent in interaction, collaboration and application. FL can offer an effective approach to addressing gender diversity by creating flexible, learner-oriented, and inclusive English language learning. In the chapter, it will be proposed to investigate how FL can be implemented in a strategic way to facilitate inclusive English language classes that recognize, see, and respond to gender diversity.</jats:p>

title: Language, Identity, and Gender in English Language Learning Spaces
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
10937901dd75497665de1150443afa014940c22d.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores the interplay between language, identity, and gender in English language learning, positioning gender as a dynamic, socially constructed element shaping learner experiences. Moving beyond binary perspectives, it highlights how gender influences motivation, participation, discourse practices, and access to resources across formal and digital contexts. Drawing on sociocultural and critical linguistic frameworks, the chapter examines how institutional structures, pedagogies, and sociocultural norms reinforce or challenge gendered inclusion. It further evaluates the role of technology in both enabling identity expression and reproducing inequalities. The study advocates for gender-responsive pedagogies that promote equity, inclusivity, and learner agency. Ultimately, it contributes to rethinking English language education as an empowering and socially just space for diverse gender identities.</jats:p>

title: Predicting Students' Engagement in English Classes Taught by Female Teachers
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
005ef4918eb28d6dd8d8be8be38225ef572fc00d.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the influence of female teacher–related factors on engineering students' engagement in English classes. The objective was to identify and predict the key determinants contributing to students' active participation and attentiveness. A quantitative cross-sectional design was adopted, and data were collected from 386 engineering students using a structured questionnaire. Exploratory Factor Analysis validated the underlying constructs, followed by Multiple Regression Analysis to determine significant predictors. Machine Learning techniques, including classification, clustering, and feature ranking, were applied to enhance predictive accuracy. The findings revealed that communication comfort, supportive classroom practices, and mentoring sensitivity were stronger determinants of engagement than role model influence or anxiety reduction. The study highlights the importance of participatory and inclusive teaching practices in fostering engagement in female-led English classrooms.</jats:p>

title: Sociotechnical Production of English Proficiency in EFL and ESL Learning Ecologies
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
e7191931036f740ec255978fc606e47178657fdb.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter develops a conceptual framework for understanding English proficiency in EFL and ESL contexts as a sociotechnically produced, gender-mediated, and ecologically distributed achievement. Moving beyond binary and deficit logics, it synthesizes gender theory, language acquisition theory, motivation theory, identity theory, assessment theory, and platform governance to show how opportunity structures, participation economies, recognition regimes, affective climates, and institutional architectures shape linguistic development. The chapter theorizes gender as a multiscalar force structuring access to input, output, feedback, legitimacy, and mobility. It advances a framework for gender-responsive pedagogy, fair assessment, and inclusive digital governance, positioning English education as a site of epistemic justice, instructional integrity, and policy design within globally stratified learning ecologies.</jats:p>

title: Teacher Beliefs, Identity, and Gender in Language Education
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
df53dd01a598067c8ee6e55e03d0e8baa6457500.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the intricate interconnections between teacher beliefs, professional identity formation, and gender dynamics in language education contexts. Drawing on contemporary research from 2021-2025, the analysis explores how language teachers' cognitions, self-perceptions, and gendered experiences shape pedagogical practices and classroom interactions. The chapter synthesizes empirical evidence across diverse educational settings, revealing how teacher beliefs influence identity construction, how professional identities are negotiated through gendered lenses, and how these elements collectively impact English language teaching effectiveness. Key findings d``emonstrate that teacher beliefs about language learning, instructional approaches, and student capabilities are deeply intertwined with identity tensions, particularly for early-career educators and those navigating intersectional identities.</jats:p>

title: Voices, Silences, and Agency
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
d0ba0e1a0f0b6b48c4fd163cca2a870ecd1f4443.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines gendered classroom discourse and advances a model of gender-responsive pedagogy in Indo-Iranian EFL/ESL contexts. Drawing on sociocultural theory, feminist pedagogy, critical applied linguistics, and postcolonial perspectives, it explores how gender shapes learner participation, voice, and agency. Using classroom observations, teacher narratives, and learner reflections, the study highlights patterns of silence, turn-taking, authority, and resistance, emphasizing the socially constructed nature of gender differences. The chapter proposes context-sensitive pedagogical strategies, including dialogic tasks, equitable interaction, collaborative learning, and textbook interrogation, offering actionable guidance for fostering inclusive, reflective, and empowering English language classrooms.</jats:p>

title: Young racialized deaf/hard of hearing adults’ interactions with speech-language pathologists
container-title: Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education
9c05facf3dccb34d97475500595dd2c37d97f7e3.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Marginalized experiences have typically been excluded within healthcare. This critical qualitative arts-based study sought to elevate the expressions of young adults who identify as deaf/hard of hearing, and Racialized, Black, Indigenous and/or People of Color and to learn about their interactions with speech-language pathologists (SLPs). This research, grounded in Dis/ability Critical Race Theory and Crip Linguistics, used multiple case studies. Participant expressions of actual and preferred interactions were elicited and analyzed through digital collage and semi-structured interviews. This study revealed that actual interactions lacked attunement between the service user and the SLP and that the SLP did not sufficiently support service users’ social connections. It also revealed preferred interactions in the form of supporting Deaf culture and providing modality options, including in minoritized languages, and supporting service user confidence. These findings have relevant implications for the SLP field related to clinical teaching, practice, research, policy, and paradigm shifts.</jats:p>

title: CogniPaz, an Ecologically Oriented Gamified mHealth Tool for Detecting Mild Cognitive Impairment: Prospective Cohort Diagnostic Accuracy Study
container-title: JMIR mHealth and uHealth
5e441833bc2d296fe5085af9f436bc7fe5119c70.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Discriminating mild cognitive impairment (MCI) from subjective cognitive decline (SCD), and healthy controls (HC) remains challenging. Digital tools may overcome paper-and-pencil screening’s limitations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and usability of CogniPaz (Daniel Blanco), an ecologically oriented, mobile health (mHealth), gamified cognitive assessment tool exploring memory and executive functions, in discriminating MCI (particularly amnestic phenotypes [aMCI]) from SCD, and HC.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This prospective observational study recruited a convenience sample of consecutive patients with cognitive complaints and HC at La Paz University Hospital Cognitive Disorders Unit from April 2025 to January 2026. Demographic and clinical characteristics, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores were collected. An evaluator blinded to the MoCA scores oversaw the automated, self-administered CogniPaz assessment. Participants were classified into HC (no cognitive complaints, MoCA score≥26), SCD (cognitive complaints, MoCA score≥26), and MCI (cognitive complaints without functional impairment, MoCA score<26, subdivided into amnestic [aMCI] and nonamnestic phenotypes). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses using age-adjusted models, the DeLong test, and bootstrap validation evaluated diagnostic accuracy across groups. The correlation between MoCA and CogniPaz scores was assessed using Spearman rank correlation. Participants with available biomarker data underwent exploratory analysis of CogniPaz’s ability to detect biologically confirmed any-cause neurodegeneration (bND). Usability was tested using an ad hoc Likert questionnaire (1‐9 points).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The participants (n=84, 57.1% female; median age 72.0, IQR 62.5-77.0 years) included 27 HC, 17 with SCD, 22 with aMCI, and 18 with nonamnestic MCI. The aMCI group was older than the SCD group (age: median 76.5, IQR 70.8-78.8 vs median 59.0, IQR 50.0-69.0 years; Kruskal-Wallis/Dunn,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.003). CogniPaz scores correlated with MoCA scores (ρ
                      <jats:italic>=</jats:italic>
                      0.81, 95% CI 0.75‐0.89;
                      <jats:italic>P<</jats:italic>
                      .001). CogniPaz showed good concurrent accuracy, independently of age: MCI vs HC (area under the curve [AUC]=0.880, 95% CI 0.798‐0.961), MCI vs SCD (AUC=0.915, 95% CI 0.841‐0.990), aMCI vs HC (AUC=0.910, 95% CI 0.830‐0.990), and aMCI vs SCD (AUC=0.943, 95% CI 0.878‐1.000). At the provisional <28.5 cutoff point, sensitivity ranged from 85.0% (34/40, 95% CI 70.2‐94.3) to 90.9% (20/22, 95% CI 70.8‐98.9) and specificity from 74.1% (20/27, 95% CI 53.7‐88.9) to 82.4% (14/17, 95% CI 56.6‐96.2) across comparisons. CogniPaz suggested capacity to detect bND (AUC=0.810, 95% CI 0.661‐0.958), with potential incremental value over MoCA and age (odds ratio [OR]=0.78, 95% CI 0.60‐0.94;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.02). Median administration time was 9.39 (IQR 7.53‐11.38) minutes with 100% (84/84) completion. User satisfaction was high (median score 8.4/9, IQR 7.9‐8.6; Cronbach α=0.84).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>CogniPaz is an innovative, user-friendly mHealth tool that addresses classical cognitive screening tools’ limitations through a brief, multidomain, minimally supervised gamified format, with high patient acceptance. It correlates with MoCA scores, shows good concurrent capacity to differentiate MCI, particularly aMCI, from SCD and HC, and appears promising for identifying bND. Pending external longitudinal validation, these findings support CogniPaz as a candidate for early cognitive screening in primary care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Communication Changes Following SPEAK OUT!: Perspectives of People With Parkinson's Disease and Their Care Partners
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
065dde955dc592e7de204a31829ba6f6e54e7cc9.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The purpose of this study was to examine whether the SPEAK OUT!® Therapy Program impacts patient self-reported outcomes in communicative effectiveness and voice function for people with Parkinson's disease (PwPD) and hypokinetic dysarthria and to identify patient factors (e.g., cognition, dysarthria severity) that influence treatment response. In addition, we examined how care partners perceived changes in PwPD's communicative effectiveness following SPEAK OUT! and how self-ratings and care partner ratings compared to each other.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-seven PwPD completed the SPEAK OUT! Therapy Program via telehealth. Two patient-reported outcome measures (i.e., Communication Effectiveness Survey [CES] and Voice Handicap Index-10 [VHI-10]) were collected at three pretreatment and three posttreatment timepoints. A subset of 13 PwPD had care partners who also provided CES ratings at pre- and posttreatment timepoints. Linear mixed-effects models were used to determine whether CES and VHI-10 scores significantly changed following treatment, to identify individual factors that influenced treatment response, and to assess alignment between PwPD's self-rated CES scores and care partner CES scores at pre- and posttreatment timepoints.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>PwPD's self-rated CES scores and VHI-10 scores significantly improved between pretreatment and posttreatment timepoints. Three individual factors—Montreal Cognitive Assessment score, dysarthria severity, and homework completion—significantly influenced treatment gains in CES and/or VHI-10 scores. Alignment between PwPD self-rated CES scores and care partner CES ratings did not change between pretreatment and posttreatment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings provide preliminary support for the effectiveness of the SPEAK OUT! Therapy Program in improving self-perceived communicative effectiveness and voice function for PwPD. This study is also the first to demonstrate positive outcomes of the program administered via telehealth. These findings provide preliminary comparisons of PwPD and care partner perspectives throughout the therapy program.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Supplemental Material:</jats:title>

                    </jats:p>
